region: Pelvic girdle, thigh, leg and foot
note: Serial correspondences to forelimb muscles are recorded in `homology.serial`. Following Diogo & Molnar (2014), a listed correspondence is a claim of TOPOLOGICAL equivalence only. It is not a claim of serial homology in the strict (ancestral-duplication) sense, and in several documented cases the two muscles derive from different anlagen.

muscles.name: Puboischiofemoralis internus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) mass of the pelvic limb bud.
synonyms: puboischiofemoralis internus A–D (Prikryl et al. 2009 letter codes, anurans)

consensus.origin: Internal (medial) surface of the pubis and ilium, and the ventral surfaces of the posterior trunk vertebrae.
consensus.insertion: Proximal femur, on or near the trochanter.
consensus.action: Protracts (flexes) and medially rotates the femur; the principal hip protractor of sprawling tetrapods.
consensus.innervation: Femoral nerve (L2–L4) and direct branches of the lumbar plexus.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis internus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Passes anterior to the ilium to reach the hip. The pubo-ischiac plate is the fused ventral pelvic plate; it is scored here as pubis plus ischium, following the paper's own gloss of the ischium as the plate's posterior portion.
occurrences.origin: Internal (dorsal) face of the pubo-ischiac plate.
occurrences.insertion: Extensively on the femur — the anterior face, extending dorsally and ventrally — anterior to the puboischiofemoralis externus.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis internus A–D
occurrences.note: Prikryl et al. (2009) letter codes are used deliberately in place of the mammalian-sounding names ('iliacus', 'sartorius', 'pectineus') that earlier authors applied to these muscles, because those names imply homologies that do not hold. The anuran iliacus externus and internus belong to this field. Note the unresolved 'pectineus' — Noble (1922) placed it here, others in the externus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. Iliacus internus and externus, which between them are this record's anuran occurrence. Internus arises on the inner surface of the ilium opposite the anterior acetabulum — variably instead on the anterior rounded margin of the acetabular portion — runs over the anterior acetabular margin and inserts along the proximal anteroventral femur beneath the iliacus externus. Externus arises on the iliac shaft.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis internus (PIFI 2)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Reconstructed at Witmer inference level I over a muscular scar on the craniolateral face of the greater trochanter, on the proximolateral tuberosity of the femur.

occurrences.name: M. iliofemoralis internus + iliotrochantericus cranialis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian puboischiofemoralis internus 1-2. Hip flexors and medial rotators; Allen et al. find hip medial-rotator moment arms roughly doubling along the bird line.

occurrences.name: Iliacus + psoas major (+ sartorius)
occurrences.action: Flexes the hip; the principal hip flexor.
occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar follow Walker & Homberger (1997) in deriving the mammalian sartorius from the ANTERIOR HEAD of puboischiofemoralis internus — not from the reptilian 'ambiens', as is commonly stated.

parts.name: Sartorius
parts.note: Diogo & Molnar follow Walker & Homberger (1997) in deriving it from the anterior head of this muscle, against the common claim that it comes from the reptilian 'ambiens'.

occurrences.attachmentNote: Iliopsoas: the psoas major head from the ventrolateral bodies and transverse-process bases of the last two or three lumbar vertebrae, the iliacus head from the arcuate line and ventral margin of the ilium, the two fusing before a common insertion on the lesser trochanter and secondarily the femoral neck. The sartorius, which this record's Theria occurrence also carries, runs instead from the iliac wing to the patella and the medial cnemial crest, and its rows are not merged in here.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis internus
occurrences.action: Protracts the femur; the posterodorsal part also abducts the leg.

parts.name: Anteroventral part
parts.note: Gadow and Kriegler's equivalent of part I in lizards. From most of the dorsal pubis and the epipubic cartilage, interdigitating across the midline with its counterpart.

parts.name: Posterodorsal part
parts.note: Homologous with part III of lizards. From most of the medial ilium, the underside of the first sacral rib and vertebra, and two presacral vertebrae.

occurrences.divisionNote: Two parts often treated as separate muscles. Both converge and unite anterior to the acetabulum before a common insertion, so the division is at the origin only.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta — Walker (1973) writes *Pseudemys scripta*. **The morphological dorsal surface of the turtle femur faces anteriorly**, which is why a muscle inserting dorsally acts as a protractor; the row records the surface and the note records what that means. In pleurodires, where the ventral girdle is reduced and fused to the shell, much of this origin has spread onto the plastron anterior to the pubis — the same shell-as-attachment pattern as the forelimb.

occurrences.name: Iliopsoas
occurrences.action: Flexes the thigh at the hip; psoas major also flexes the trunk.
occurrences.innervation: Femoral nerve, and direct branches of the ventral rami of L1-L4.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Iliacus from the iliac fossa, iliac crest and ala of the sacrum; psoas major from the bodies and transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae; the two join in one tendon onto the lesser trochanter. **The lumbar origin is the change.** In a lizard this muscle is a pelvic muscle taking origin inside the pelvic canal; in a human a whole half of it has climbed onto the vertebral column, which is what lets it flex the trunk as well as the thigh. Psoas minor is scored as a third part and ends on the pelvis rather than the femur — a limb muscle that stopped short of the limb.

homology.notes: A stable row across Tetrapoda. Its subdivision in mammals into iliacus, psoas major and sartorius is a derived elaboration.

serial.caution: Topological correspondence only — the pelvic and pectoral internal girdle muscles were not acquired at the same time.

homology.teaching: The sartorius derivation is a good correction to a widespread textbook claim.

muscles.name: Puboischiofemoralis externus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral (flexor) mass.

consensus.origin: External (lateral/ventral) surfaces of the pubis and ischium.
consensus.insertion: Proximal femur, ventrally.
consensus.action: Adducts and laterally rotates the femur.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis externus
occurrences.note: Deeply blended with the 'pubofemoralis' (= adductor femoris) in Necturus (Walker 1954).
occurrences.attachmentNote: An insertion covering two-thirds of the femoral shaft. Extensive fleshy attachments like this one are why femoral muscle scars in salamanders are poor guides to muscle boundaries.
occurrences.origin: Much of the ventral surface of the pubo-ischiac plate.
occurrences.insertion: Ventral surface of the femur, over nearly two-thirds of the bone's length.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis externus
occurrences.note: Přikryl et al. (2009) note that the anuran 'pectineus' was identified as puboischiofemoralis EXTERNUS by Hoffmann (1873-78) and Iordansky & Morozov (1994), but as puboischiofemoralis INTERNUS by Noble (1922). The primary literature disagrees about which of the two it is, not merely about what to call it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. Scored from the muscle Prikryl et al. call the pectineus, which Hoffmann and Iordansky & Morozov call the puboischiofemoralis externus — one of the twelve or so anuran names that mean something different in the mammalian literature. Ischium to femur; the review table does not resolve either end further.

occurrences.name: M. obturatorius lateralis + medialis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian puboischiofemoralis externus 1-3.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis externus
occurrences.note: Reconstructed from the ventral pelvic plate and the trochanteric region; its relative size is one of the variables Bishop & Pierce use to infer posture.

occurrences.name: Obturator externus, quadratus femoris, gemelli
occurrences.action: Laterally rotates the thigh; stabilises the hip.
occurrences.divisionNote: The gemelli are claimed by this field and by the ischiotrochantericus; the dataset records both claims.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Three muscles on one field. Obturator externus from the cranial, ventral and caudal margins of the obturator foramen on the lateral pelvis to the deep trochanteric fossa; quadratus femoris from the caudal lateral ischium to the caudodistal greater trochanter and distolateral fossa; gemelli from the ischial tuberosity and ischial body to the proximal fossa. All three reach the hip joint capsule.

occurrences.name: Obturator externus, quadratus femoris and the gemelli
occurrences.action: Laterally rotate the thigh; obturator externus also adducts it.
occurrences.innervation: Obturator nerve to obturator externus; nerve to quadratus femoris and nerve to obturator internus to the remainder.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Obturator externus from the external surface of the obturator membrane and both pubic rami to the trochanteric fossa; quadratus femoris from the lateral ischial tuberosity to the quadrate line; the two gemelli from the ischial spine and tuberosity onto the obturator internus tendon. **Three of the four names here are on Diogo & Molnar's list of false friends** — 'obturator externus', 'quadratus femoris' and 'gemellus' are all applied to non-homologous muscles in the anuran literature. The gemelli are the oddity: they do not reach the femur at all, inserting instead on another muscle's tendon.

homology.notes: The obturator nerve is the constant marker for this field across Tetrapoda.

muscles.name: Iliofemoralis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass.

consensus.insertion: Proximal femur, on or near the greater trochanter.
consensus.action: Abducts the femur; in erect-limbed taxa, the principal hip abductor and pelvic stabiliser during single-limb support.

occurrences.name: Iliofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. Shares its origin on the posterolateral tuber superius with the iliofibularis — the two are slender and closely bound — and inserts on the dorsal surface of the crista femoralis, the crest running posteriorly from the proximal femur. Both ends are on named anuran processes, so this is one of the few thigh muscles here that leaves a correlate at each end.

occurrences.name: Iliofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the anterior iliac blade, sharing an intramuscular septum with the puboischiotibialis; the belly wraps the posterior femoral border to insert proximally. Femur abductor, active in swing.

occurrences.name: Iliofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Tendinous origin on the central lateral ilium, deep to iliotibialis 2; inserts fleshy onto the DISTAL THIRD of the dorso-lateral femur, between femorotibialis internus and externus, and attaches along most of the femoral length. The femorotibialis internus tendon arising distal and anterior to it is the landmark Klinkhamer et al. use to separate the two. Hip abductor, confirmed by EMG. This is the description `extensor-iliotibialis` was also carrying.

occurrences.name: M. iliofemoralis externus
occurrences.note: Hip abductor.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Iliofemoralis
occurrences.note: Its expansion, tracked through the enlargement of the iliac blade, is central to Bishop & Pierce's argument that erect hindlimb posture was acquired late in the therian stem lineage.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Expansion of the iliac blade along the synapsid stem tracks the enlargement of this field and the shift toward erect posture.

occurrences.name: Gluteus medius + gluteus minimus
occurrences.action: Abduct and medially rotate the thigh; prevent pelvic drop during the stance phase.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Same muscle, same nerve, same attachments — but in a parasagittal limb it becomes the principal pelvic stabiliser during single-limb support.

occurrences.name: Iliofemoralis
occurrences.action: Abducts and protracts the femur.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Covers most of the dorsolateral pelvis lateral and posterior to the posterodorsal head of the puboischiofemoralis internus. Extensive origin from the first sacral and one or two presacral vertebrae, **the adjacent carapace**, and most of the lateral surface and anterior border of the ilium, converging onto the dorsal surface of the trochanter major. Most turtles resemble *Pseudemys* in taking some fibres from the vertebrae as well as the ilium.

occurrences.name: Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
occurrences.action: Abduct the thigh and stabilise the pelvis over the stance limb.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Medius from the external ilium between the posterior and anterior gluteal lines, minimus between the anterior and inferior lines, both onto the greater trochanter. **This record's whole point is visible here**: the transformation from a modest abductor in a sprawling limb to the principal pelvic stabiliser in a parasagittal one happens with no change of identity, origin, insertion or nerve — the same bone, the same trochanter, the same superior gluteal supply, doing a different job because the limb is held differently. Tensor fasciae latae is scored as a disputed part: it shares the superior gluteal nerve with the other two, but its insertion on the iliotibial tract puts it as easily in the iliotibialis field, and this dataset does not resolve that.

homology.notes: Universal in Tetrapoda. The functional transformation — from a modest abductor in a sprawling limb to the principal pelvic stabiliser in a parasagittal one — happens without any change in identity, origin, insertion or nerve.
homology.teaching: The best single muscle for showing that posture change is a change in mechanics, not in anatomy. Same muscle, same nerve, radically different role.
homology.caveat: Leavey et al. (2024), using diceCT on 30 frog species across five locomotor modes, report that bone lengths and pelvic crest sizes are generally NOT reliable predictors of muscle size, and find many-to-one form-function mapping. That is a direct caution against reading muscle proportions off skeletal proportions in fossils, which is the inference osteological correlates are usually recruited for. Correlates locate an attachment; they do not size the muscle that made it.

muscles.name: Caudofemoralis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; derived from the caudal axial musculature, not from the limb bud proper.

consensus.origin: Ventrolateral surfaces of the caudal vertebrae and their transverse processes (longus); the posterolateral ilium (brevis).
consensus.insertion: Fourth trochanter of the femur.
consensus.action: The principal femoral retractor of non-mammalian tetrapods — the main propulsive muscle of the hindlimb in sprawling and archosaurian locomotion.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the caudal spinal nerves; inferior gluteal nerve territory in mammals.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: The origin has a countable segmental address — caudals four and five — which is rare in this dataset and is what makes the caudofemoralis tractable in fossils. The insertion is given as the femoral crista ventralis; whether that ridge is the same structure as the amniote fourth trochanter is not settled here, so no landmark is asserted.
occurrences.origin: Transverse processes of the fourth and fifth caudal vertebrae.
occurrences.insertion: Crista ventralis of the femur, by a strong tendon.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis longus + brevis
occurrences.action: Primary femoral retractor; drives the propulsive stroke in lizard locomotion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Longus arises from the proximal third of the tail and caudal vertebrae 4-14, inserting by broad tendon on the femoral trochanter plus a second tendon onto the lateral menisci of the knee; brevis arises from the transverse processes of the four most anterior postsacral vertebrae. Femur retraction and long-axis rotation, active in stance.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis
occurrences.note: Inferred from a low, proximodistally elongate fourth trochanter about a quarter of the way down the posteromedial femur, bearing a shallow medial pit. Level I inference. Its modest development relative to the crocodylian condition is the observation that bears on how much of locomotion was still tail-driven in the sphenosuchian grade.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: A rough convexity identified as the fourth trochanter, continuing distally as a faint ridge bearing insertion scars.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis longus + brevis
occurrences.note: Large and well developed; inserts on a prominent fourth trochanter. Attachments are deliberately not scored for Alligator mississippiensis: Allen et al. measure this muscle's architecture but give no attachment sites (0.1 origin/insertion mentions per page), and Diogo & Molnar's crocodylian exemplar is Caiman latirostris. The rows this occurrence used to carry were Klinkhamer et al.'s description of Crocodylus porosus and have moved to their own occurrence.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis longus + brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Longus is fleshy from the haemal arches of numerous caudal vertebrae BEGINNING AT CAUDAL VERTEBRA 12; brevis has TWO heads, one from the postero-lateral ilium and one from caudal vertebrae 4 and 5, anterior to the longus origin — so both muscles take caudal vertebrae and the caudal row is shared, where the block used to read longus-from-vertebrae and brevis-from-ilium as though each had one head. Both insert by tendon on the proximo-ventral femur at the fourth trochanter. The second insertion row is the longus' ACCESSORY TENDON onto the ventro-distal femur at the tibial condyle, together with gastrocnemius externus; scored on the condyles because that is as fine as skeleton.json resolves. The longus is the largest muscle in the animal's body. Allen et al. is no longer cited here: it measures architecture and gives no attachment sites, and it is the Alligator source that used to hold this row on the wrong animal.

occurrences.name: M. caudofemoralis pars caudalis + pars pelvica
occurrences.note: Greatly reduced with the shortening of the tail to the pygostyle and the shift to a knee-driven, femur-held-horizontal gait. Its reduction is a defining event in the theropod–bird locomotor transition. Allen et al. (2021) split the avian muscle into pars caudalis (= crocodylian caudofemoralis longus) and pars pelvica (= brevis). Its leverage declines across several nodes along the bird line.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis
occurrences.note: Progressive reduction along the synapsid stem, tracked through the reduction of the fourth trochanter.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Progressive reduction of the fourth trochanter along the synapsid stem tracks the loss of tail-driven femoral retraction.

occurrences.note: Galictis cuja. Ercoli et al. state it flatly: 'M. gluteofemoralis (m. caudofemoralis) — this muscle is absent.' A carnivoran with a long, well-muscled tail, where a persistent gluteofemoralis would be least surprising, and it is not there; they read the absence as a derived condition acquired within some mustelid clades. In THREE HIND LIMBS the caudal portion of the gluteus superficialis divided into one or more extra bellies, which they suggest 'could be a remnant of this muscle' — a second candidate remnant, and one that disagrees with the proposal that the piriformis is the remnant. The paper gives no denominator for those three limbs, and this note previously said 'three of six', which the paper does not support: its methods name three specimens plus a fourth for additional observations, and its largest stated count anywhere is 'in four legs'. This row read `variable` until an audit caught it — that was the clade's answer written onto one animal, which is the error the rollup exists to prevent. Theria computes `variable` on its own if another therian disagrees.

occurrences.name: Piriformis
occurrences.action: Laterally rotates the extended thigh; abducts the flexed thigh.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Anterior surface of the sacrum to the upper border of the greater trochanter. **Scored on a proposed correspondence, and the proposal is about a lost tail.** This record tracks the fourth trochanter, which is what makes it the most reliably reconstructed hindlimb muscle in fossils; the human femur has no fourth trochanter and the human tail is a coccyx, so what survives is a short sacrum-to-trochanter muscle that has kept the topology and lost the lever. Birds and anurans reduced the same muscle independently, for the same reason.

homology.notes: Presence and size track the fourth trochanter directly, making this the most reliably reconstructed hindlimb muscle in fossils. Its independent reduction in birds and in mammals accompanies two separate shifts away from tail-driven femoral retraction. Anurans are a third such reduction and the most complete: with the tail lost and the caudal series replaced by the urostyle, the muscle's origin has no vertebrae to arise from.

serial.caution: No forelimb counterpart. The caudofemoralis is a clean falsification of any expectation of one-to-one fore/hindlimb correspondence.

homology.teaching: The single best fossil-muscle example: a bony landmark (the fourth trochanter) that reads directly as muscle presence, size and locomotor mode across 300 million years.
homology.caveat: Leavey et al. (2024), using diceCT on 30 frog species across five locomotor modes, report that bone lengths and pelvic crest sizes are generally NOT reliable predictors of muscle size, and find many-to-one form-function mapping. That is a direct caution against reading muscle proportions off skeletal proportions in fossils, which is the inference osteological correlates are usually recruited for. Correlates locate an attachment; they do not size the muscle that made it.

muscles.name: Extensor iliotibialis / iliotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass.

consensus.insertion: Tibia, via the knee extensor apparatus.
consensus.action: Extends the knee; protracts the femur.

occurrences.name: Extensor iliotibialis
occurrences.note: Single-headed in Taricha, against the two heads (pars anterior and posterior) usual in Cryptobranchus, Necturus, Salamandra, Pseudoeurycea, Ambystoma and Dicamptodon. The split tracks limb robustness rather than habitat or phylogeny: slender-limbed salamanders (Amphiuma, Typhlomolge, Bolitoglossa, Taricha) have one head, robust-limbed ones two, and aquatic and terrestrial species occur in both groups. Smith (1927) reported two heads in the congener Taricha granulosa, so the character may vary within the genus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crosses both hip and knee. Recorded with a single head in Taricha; the tibial insertion is on the anterior proximal tibia, which the paper calls the spine and which may or may not be the cnemial crest of amniotes — left unasserted.
occurrences.origin: Lateral surface of the ilium above the acetabulum.
occurrences.insertion: Spine of the tibia, by a long strong tendon.

occurrences.name: Extensor iliotibialis A/B
occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar use letter codes rather than the mammalian names ('gluteus maximus', 'tensor fasciae latae') applied by earlier authors, because those homologies do not hold. Přikryl et al. (2009) list the anuran muscle as 'glutaeus maximus (iliotibialis)'. It is NOT homologous with the mammalian gluteus maximus — one of the twelve false-friend names Diogo & Molnar (2014) identify.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. Cruralis and glutaeus maximus, this record's anuran A/B pair. Cruralis runs from the ilium to the knee aponeurosis; glutaeus maximus from the dorsolateral tuber superius onto the fascia of the distal cruralis rather than onto bone. Prikryl et al. note the glutaeus maximus origin is the one marked on their pelvic figure — it is a scoreable correlate.

occurrences.name: Iliotibialis (+ femorotibialis, + 'ambiens')
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. The whole knee-extensor field this record covers in lizards: iliotibialis from the lateral ilium by a broad aponeurosis, 'ambiens' aponeurotically from the pubis and proximoventral femur, femorotibialis from the femoral shaft by four bellies surrounding it. All three converge tendinously on the lateral surface of the tibial condyle.

occurrences.name: Iliotibialis 1 and 2
occurrences.attachmentNote: Rugosities on the dorsal surface of the supraacetabular crest. Godoy et al. note the surface is unusually extensively rugose in P. sera, implying a larger attachment area than in comparable notosuchians.

occurrences.name: Iliotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Three parts, and all three insert by tendon on the PROXIMO-ANTERIOR TIBIA: IT1 fleshy from the antero-lateral ilium, IT2 by tendon from the central lateral ilium between IT1 and IT3, IT3 fleshy from the postero-lateral ilium. IT2 is the largest and forms almost the whole dorsolateral face of the thigh. All three are knee extensors, which is what a tibial insertion is for, and EMG confirms it for IT2.

occurrences.name: M. iliotibialis cranialis + lateralis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian iliotibialis 1-3.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Rectus femoris + tensor fasciae latae
occurrences.action: Extends the knee; flexes the hip.
occurrences.innervation: Femoral nerve; superior gluteal nerve (tensor fasciae latae).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Rectus femoris from the quadriceps tuberosity of the ilium and the cranial hip capsule to the anterodorsal patellar margin; tensor fasciae latae from a small area of the iliac wing, inserting not on bone but through the fascia lata onto gluteus superficialis, biceps femoris, sartorius and the crural fascia.

occurrences.name: Iliotibialis (+ femorotibialis, + 'ambiens')
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Iliotibialis
occurrences.action: Extends the shank; also abducts and possibly retracts the femur.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Band-shaped, its main origin on the posterodorsal corner of the ilium dorsal to the iliofibularis origin, plus a **second tendinous head in *Pseudemys*** from the anterior border of the ilium. Sitting high on the ilium it can abduct and retract the femur as well as extend the shank.

occurrences.name: Rectus femoris
occurrences.action: Extends the knee and flexes the hip.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Straight head from the anterior inferior iliac spine, reflected head from above the acetabular rim, to the patella and the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament. **The rectus femoris is why the quadriceps is a composite of two different ancestral muscles**: it comes from this record and the three vasti come from the femorotibialis, which is exactly why the rectus crosses the hip and the vasti do not. Read the two rows together — one human muscle group, two homology groups, and the joint each part spans is the tell. The urodele end of this record is actively disputed: Kardong derives femorotibialis, iliotibialis and 'ambiens' from three separate salamander muscles, Gadow, Walker and Diogo & Molnar from one.

homology.notes: The urodele/reptile correspondence is actively disputed. Kardong (2002) derives the reptilian femorotibialis, iliotibialis and 'ambiens' from three distinct salamander muscles; Gadow (1882), Walker (1954) and Diogo & Molnar derive all three from a single salamander extensor iliotibialis. The dissections in Diogo & Molnar (2014) support the latter.
homology.openQuestion: One salamander muscle or three? The answer changes how many separate acquisitions are needed in the reptile lineage.

serial.caution: Both are the principal extensor of the second limb joint, but the correspondence is functional and topological, not developmental.

homology.caveat: Leavey et al. (2024), using diceCT on 30 frog species across five locomotor modes, report that bone lengths and pelvic crest sizes are generally NOT reliable predictors of muscle size, and find many-to-one form-function mapping. That is a direct caution against reading muscle proportions off skeletal proportions in fossils, which is the inference osteological correlates are usually recruited for. Correlates locate an attachment; they do not size the muscle that made it.

muscles.name: Iliofibularis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) mass.

consensus.origin: Lateral surface of the ilium, posterior to the iliofemoralis origin.
consensus.insertion: Proximal fibula, via a broad tendon.
consensus.action: Extends the hip and flexes the knee; stabilises the femur during the stance phase.

occurrences.name: M. iliofibularis
occurrences.note: Tomańska et al. (2025) report it stabilising the pelvic region and femur during movement in Varanus komodoensis, allowing hip abduction. Dick & Clemente (2016) include it among the major varanid locomotor muscles.

occurrences.name: M. iliofibularis
occurrences.note: Its insertion marks the iliofibular tubercle on the fibular shaft, which Pereyra et al. (2024) use as the landmark for the fibularis longus origin.

occurrences.name: M. iliofibularis
occurrences.note: Name retained across the crocodylian–avian transition. Allen et al. (2021) find knee-flexor leverage declining relative to knee extensors along the bird line, which is the leverage change underlying the shift from hip-driven to knee-driven propulsion.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: iliofibularis
occurrences.note: Present in anurans under the same name; Přikryl et al. (2009) describe it attaching to the knee aponeurosis, partly covering the head of the fibula.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. The dorsal member of the iliofibularis/iliofemoralis pair, sharing their origin on the tuber superius. Its distal half is exposed and attaches into the knee aponeurosis, in part covering the head of the fibula — so the fibular attachment is by way of the aponeurosis rather than directly onto bone.

occurrences.name: Iliofibularis
occurrences.action: Elevates the femur and flexes the knee.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Runs parallel to the extensor iliotibialis but slightly deeper and posterior, crossing both hip and knee. The insertion is the site the iliofibular tubercle marks in taxa that have one; no landmark is asserted here because the paper does not name a tubercle.
occurrences.origin: External face of the ilium, just posterior to the extensor iliotibialis.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior side of the proximal end of the fibula, by a tendon.

homology.notes: One of the muscles whose name survives unchanged from crocodylians to birds in Allen et al.'s (2021) table. Its correspondence with the mammalian biceps femoris is proposed but not settled — Diogo & Molnar (2014) treat the hamstring group as deriving from the ischioflexorius field rather than from a single iliofibularis.
homology.openQuestion: Is the amniote iliofibularis the homologue of the mammalian biceps femoris, or does the hamstring group derive wholesale from the ischioflexorius field?
homology.teaching: A muscle spanning hip and knee whose declining leverage is measurable along the bird line — a case where a function claim rests on geometry, not on presence or absence.

muscles.name: Femorotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass.
synonyms: vastus lateralis + vastus medialis + vastus intermedius (mammals)

consensus.insertion: Tibia, via the knee extensor apparatus.
consensus.action: Extends the knee. Because it does not cross the hip, it is a pure knee extensor.

occurrences.note: Not separated from the extensor iliotibialis in salamanders under the Gadow/Walker/Diogo & Molnar reading.

occurrences.name: Femorotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy origin along the entire femoral shaft; joins the iliotibialis tendon to insert on the cnemial crest. Knee extensor, active in both stance and swing.

occurrences.name: Femorotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Externus arises fleshy about a third of the way down the dorsal femur and inserts on the proximo-lateral cnemial crest; internus arises by tendon on the dorso-proximal femur, distal and anterior to iliofemoralis, and joins the same tendon at insertion.

occurrences.name: M. femorotibialis lateralis + medialis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian femorotibialis externus and internus.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Vastus lateralis, medialis and intermedius
occurrences.action: Extend the knee.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. The three vasti, all femoral in origin and patellar in insertion — which is the character that separates them from the rectus femoris head of the same complex. Vastus lateralis from the cranioproximal femur medial to the greater trochanter base, to the lateral patellar margin and proximolateral tibia; vastus medialis from the craniomedial femoral neck and diaphysis to the medial and mediodistal patella.

occurrences.name: Femorotibialis (vasti medialis, internus and externus)
occurrences.action: Extends the shank.

parts.name: Vastus medialis
parts.note: Arises from and covers the morphological dorsal surface of the femur.

parts.name: Vastus internus
parts.note: From the distal border of the trochanter minor and the anteroventral femur.

parts.name: Vastus externus
parts.note: From the distal border of the trochanter major and the posteroventral femur.

occurrences.divisionNote: Trifurcate at its origin in *Pseudemys*, each part called a vastus. **The two other thigh muscles run between them**: the iliofemoralis insertion passes between the origins of vasti externus and medialis, and the puboischiofemoralis internus insertion separates medialis from internus. The three-way split is carved by what crosses it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). The deepest and most massive part of the knee-extensor complex; all three vasti converge to form the greater part of the patellar tendon.

occurrences.name: Vastus lateralis, medialis and intermedius
occurrences.action: Extend the knee; articularis genu retracts the suprapatellar bursa.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Three vasti from the anterior, lateral and medial femoral shaft and the two lips of the linea aspera, onto the patella. **One of the least contested correspondences in the hindlimb** — a femur-to-tibia extensor that never crosses the hip, in every tetrapod that has one. Articularis genu is scored as a fourth part: it is a few fibres of vastus intermedius that stop at the knee capsule instead of reaching the patella, and it is the smallest thing in this dataset that still counts as a muscle.

homology.notes: The femorotibialis → vasti correspondence is one of the least contested in the hindlimb. Together with the rectus femoris (from extensor iliotibialis) it forms the mammalian quadriceps — a composite of two different ancestral muscles, which is why the rectus femoris crosses the hip and the vasti do not.
homology.teaching: Explains a fact students memorise without understanding: why one of the four quadriceps heads flexes the hip and three do not. They are not four parts of one muscle; they are two muscles.

muscles.name: 'Ambiens'
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass. Romer (1942) and Jones (1979) emphasise that it is a DORSAL muscle despite its ventral position.

consensus.insertion: Tibia (and in some archosaurs, via the digital flexor tendons).
consensus.action: Protracts the femur and extends the knee.

occurrences.note: Not present as a separate muscle; part of the undivided extensor iliotibialis.

occurrences.name: 'Ambiens'
occurrences.note: Reptiles may have both an 'ambiens' and a 'pubifemoralis'; the two names are sometimes used as synonyms (Russell & Bauer 2008), which is a persistent source of confusion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: In Varanus komodoensis the muscle has dorsal and ventral heads; the dorsal attaches to the ventral edge of the acetabulum and the ventral lies anteriorly, both converging on the femur at the intertrochanteric fossa.

occurrences.name: 'Ambiens'
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Tendinous origin on the proximo-lateral pubis, inserting by a long tendon on the proximo-anterior tibia AT THE CNEMIAL CREST — the crest is named in the source, so it is scored rather than left at the bone. Knee extensor and hip flexor, knee extension confirmed by EMG. Klinkhamer et al. found only a SINGLE HEAD, against two in Alligator mississippiensis, but they attribute that to the sub-adult age of their specimens and of the Caiman latirostris in the earlier study that found the same — NOT to a species difference. Recorded here as an observation and explicitly not as a Crocodylus porosus character.

occurrences.name: M. ambiens
occurrences.note: In birds the ambiens tendon famously passes to the digital flexors, an arrangement once invoked (incorrectly) as an automatic perching mechanism. Hip flexor and knee extensor; the name is retained across the transition.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar reject the classical derivation of the mammalian sartorius from the 'ambiens'; they derive the sartorius from the anterior head of puboischiofemoralis internus (Walker & Homberger 1997).

occurrences.name: 'Ambiens'
occurrences.action: Adducts and protracts the thigh, and extends the shank.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). A weak muscle from the posterior part of the base of the lateral pubic process and the adjacent puboischiadic ligament, onto the patellar tendon. It crosses the hip as well as the knee. **With the thigh in its normal turtle position — morphological dorsal surface directed anteriorly — the ambiens lies along its anteroventral border**, which is not where a reader importing the lizard arrangement would look for it.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **Absent, and the note is about the muscle it is not.** The classical equation makes the amniote 'ambiens' the mammalian sartorius, and Diogo & Molnar reject it: the diagnostic is that the 'ambiens' is a DORSAL muscle sitting in a ventral position, which the sartorius is not. Gest's sartorius runs from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial tibia through the pes anserinus, on the femoral nerve, and this dataset gives it no home rather than give it a wrong one. The same rejection is why 'tensor fasciae latae' appears on Diogo & Molnar's list of false-friend names.

homology.notes: The critical diagnostic is that the 'ambiens' is a DORSAL muscle sitting in a ventral position. The amphibian 'pubifemoralis', which looks superficially similar in dorsal view, is a deep VENTRAL muscle and corresponds instead to the reptilian adductor femoris. Diogo & Molnar make this call explicitly and reject the ambiens→sartorius derivation.
homology.teaching: A worked example of using mass assignment (dorsal vs ventral) rather than position to settle a homology dispute.

muscles.name: Adductor femoris
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral mass.
synonyms: adductor magnus + adductor longus + adductor brevis (mammals)

consensus.origin: Ventral surface of the pelvic girdle (pubis and ischium).
consensus.insertion: Ventral surface of the femur.
consensus.action: Adducts and retracts the femur.
consensus.innervation: Obturator nerve (with a sciatic contribution to the adductor magnus in mammals).

occurrences.name: 'Pubifemoralis'
occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar's dissections support the amphibian 'pubifemoralis' = reptilian adductor femoris, against the alternative that it corresponds to the 'ambiens'. Both are deep ventral muscles lying just dorsal to the pubotibialis and running from the ventral girdle to the ventral femur; the 'ambiens' is dorsal.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. pubifemoralis. The three ventral pelvis-to-femur muscles are separated by their sequence along the femur rather than by distinct attachment sites — internus anterior, pubifemoralis next, externus posterior.
occurrences.origin: Anterior and ventral surface of the pubo-ischiac plate, anterior to the puboischiofemoralis externus.
occurrences.insertion: Ventral face of the femur, anterior and distal to the puboischiofemoralis externus but posterior to the puboischiofemoralis internus.

occurrences.name: Adductor femoris
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the puboischiadic ligament to the ventral femoral shaft; adducts and protracts the femur, active in both stance and swing.

occurrences.name: Adductor femoris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy at the ventrolateral ischium, tendinous at the ventromedial femur.

occurrences.name: M. puboischiofemoralis medialis + lateralis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian adductor femoris 1 and 2 respectively.

occurrences.name: Adductor magnus, longus and brevis
occurrences.action: Adduct and extend the thigh.
occurrences.innervation: Obturator nerve; the hamstring part of adductor magnus by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Adductor magnus and adductor brevis share a small origin on the caudal ramus of the pubis and the ischial ramus. Magnus inserts on the distal caudal femur in two areas just proximal to the condyles, sharing fibres with semimembranosus; brevis on the proximal third of the lateral femur. Adductor longus lies between pectineus and magnus and its origin is not scored here.

occurrences.name: Adductor magnus, longus, brevis and minimus
occurrences.action: Adduct the thigh; the ischiocondylar part of adductor magnus extends it.
occurrences.innervation: Obturator nerve, both divisions; the ischiocondylar part of adductor magnus by the tibial nerve, and pectineus by the femoral nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Four adductors from the pubic rami and the ischial tuberosity onto the linea aspera, plus pectineus from the pecten of the pubis to the pectineal line. **The nerve supply is split three ways across one mass** and each split means something: the ischiocondylar part of adductor magnus takes the tibial nerve because it belongs functionally with the hamstrings, and pectineus takes the femoral nerve — and 'pectineus' is another name on Diogo & Molnar's false-friends list. This record also resolves the first of their two contested amphibian muscles: the 'pubifemoralis' is this, not the 'ambiens' it superficially resembles in dorsal view.

homology.notes: Diogo & Molnar note that almost all amphibian–reptile ventral pelvic/thigh homologies are straightforward and consensual, with exactly two exceptions: the amphibian 'pubifemoralis' and 'ischiofemoralis'. They resolve both — pubifemoralis = adductor femoris, ischiofemoralis = ischiotrochantericus.

muscles.name: Ischiotrochantericus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass.

consensus.insertion: Trochanteric region of the proximal femur.
consensus.action: Laterally rotates the femur; stabilises the hip.
consensus.innervation: Sacral plexus branches; nerve to obturator internus in mammals.

occurrences.name: 'Ischiofemoralis'
occurrences.note: Most authors (and Diogo & Molnar) hold that the amphibian 'ischiofemoralis' corresponds to the reptilian ischiotrochantericus; Gadow (1882) was a minority voice for adductor femoris. Walker (1954, p. 94) defends the ischiotrochantericus reading.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. ischiofemoralis, and the passage that fixes the plate's composition: the paper equates the ischium with the plate's posterior portion, which is what licenses scoring the plate as pubis plus ischium throughout.
occurrences.origin: Lateral border of the ischium — the posterior portion of the pubo-ischiac plate.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior face of the head of the femur.

occurrences.name: Ischiotrochantericus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the ischial tuberosity onto the proximal edge of the trochanter; in Gekko onto its distal edge.

occurrences.name: M. ischiofemoralis
occurrences.note: Hip extensor and lateral rotator.

occurrences.name: Obturator internus (+ gemelli)
occurrences.action: Laterally rotates the extended thigh; abducts the flexed thigh.
occurrences.divisionNote: The gemelli are claimed by this field and by the puboischiofemoralis externus; the dataset records both claims.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Obturator internus from the medial surface of the obturator foramen, turning over the dorsal margin of the ischium to reach the proximal trochanteric fossa. Frequently divided into two bellies near the origin and partially fused there with the gemelli, which this dataset assigns to the puboischiofemoralis externus — the membership dispute the parts list records.

occurrences.name: Ischiotrochantericus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Inserts on the **distal** edge of the trochanter, against the proximal edge in Eublepharis.

occurrences.name: Obturator internus
occurrences.action: Laterally rotates the thigh.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Internal surface of the obturator membrane and the margin of the obturator foramen, turning through a right angle around the lesser sciatic notch to the medial greater trochanter. **The obturator internus equation is one half of a pair Diogo & Molnar resolved**: of all the amphibian-to-reptile ventral pelvic homologies they found only two contested, the 'pubifemoralis' and the 'ischiofemoralis', and they resolve the second as this muscle. Note that obturator internus and obturator externus arise from the two faces of the same membrane and belong to different homology groups.

homology.notes: One of the two contested amphibian ventral pelvic muscles resolved by Diogo & Molnar (the other being 'pubifemoralis').

muscles.name: Puboischiotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass.
synonyms: puboischiotibialis sensu Mivart 1869 and Iordansky & Morozov 1994

consensus.origin: Ventral pelvic girdle — pubis and ischium.
consensus.insertion: Medial surface of the proximal tibia.
consensus.action: Adducts the thigh and flexes the knee.

occurrences.name: Puboischiotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: The most superficial muscle over the pelvis in ventral view, divided into proximal and distal sections by a tendinous inscription at about the level of the acetabulum. Francis (1934) and Mivart (1869) describe it as an undivided sheet in Salamandra and Cryptobranchus, so the inscription is not general to salamanders.
occurrences.divisionNote: Divided into proximal and distal sections by a tendinous inscription at about the level of the acetabulum in Taricha. Francis (1934) and Mivart (1869) describe it as an undivided sheet in Salamandra and Cryptobranchus, so the inscription is not general to salamanders.
occurrences.origin: Pubo-ischiac plate, lateral to the midline.
occurrences.insertion: Anterior surface of the tibia.

occurrences.name: Gracilis major + gracilis minor
occurrences.note: Two heads in anurans versus one in mammals. Both derive from the puboischiotibialis, but via different heads — so the anuran and mammalian 'gracilis' are not straightforwardly equivalent. The anuran gracilis major is Mivart's and Iordansky & Morozov's puboischiotibialis (Přikryl et al. 2009).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. Gracilis major and gracilis minor, both ischium to knee aponeurosis. Mivart and Iordansky & Morozov call the major one the puboischiotibialis, which is this record's name.

occurrences.name: Puboischiotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the pubic tubercle and both pelvic ligaments, tendinously onto the proximal tibial shaft. Two of its three origins are ligament rather than bone, which is why it leaves little for a fossil reconstruction to find.

occurrences.name: Gracilis
occurrences.action: Adducts the thigh; flexes and medially rotates the leg.
occurrences.divisionNote: One head, against two in anurans (Prikryl et al. 2009).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gracilis: a band from the ventral pelvic symphysis, fusing cranially with the insertion of the abdominal muscles, to the craniomedial tibia just proximal to the semitendinosus insertion.

occurrences.name: Puboischiotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Gracilis
occurrences.action: Adducts the thigh and flexes the knee.
occurrences.innervation: Anterior division of the obturator nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Pubic symphysis and inferior pubic ramus to the medial surface of the tibia through the pes anserinus. **This is the single most important human row in the hindlimb.** Diogo & Molnar single out the gracilis as the one muscle for which the last common ancestor of tetrapods probably had a directly corresponding individual muscle in the modern human sense — everything else in the human hindlimb is a subdivision or a recombination of something that was not a discrete muscle. If a reader wants one row that shows what a one-to-one homology looks like against a whole limb of composites, it is this one.

homology.notes: Diogo & Molnar single out the gracilis as the one muscle for which the last common ancestor of tetrapods probably had a directly corresponding individual muscle in the modern human sense — the muscles printed in bold in their Table 1. Every other human hindlimb muscle is a subdivision or recombination.
homology.teaching: A one-line answer to 'which of my leg muscles would a salamander recognise?' — essentially just the gracilis.

muscles.name: Ischioflexorius / flexor tibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass.
synonyms: semitendinosus + semimembranosus + biceps femoris (mammals — the hamstrings)

consensus.insertion: Proximal tibia and/or fibula; in some taxa continuing to the tarsus.
consensus.action: Flexes the knee and retracts (extends) the hip.

occurrences.name: Ischioflexorius
occurrences.attachmentNote: Runs from the pelvis to the sole without a bony insertion — the longest muscle chain in the hindlimb, and one whose action cannot be read from any single joint.
occurrences.note: Only the distal section is fully separable from the puboischiotibialis in Taricha; the proximal section is incompletely divided from it and resists mechanical separation. Pseudoeurycea, Bolitoglossa, Paramesotriton and Onychodactylus share this. The character does not follow salamander phylogeny and must have arisen or been lost more than once.
occurrences.origin: Posterior and lateral edge of the ischium, behind the puboischiotibialis.
occurrences.insertion: Plantar aponeurosis overlying the flexor primordialis communis.

occurrences.name: 'Semitendinosus'
occurrences.note: A false-friend name. The anuran 'semitendinosus' is not homologous to the mammalian muscle of that name. Přikryl et al. (2009) record that the anuran 'semimembranosus' was called ischioflexorius by Hoffmann and caudalipuboischiotibialis by Francis, while the anuran 'semitendinosus' was called ischioflexorius by Mivart and puboischiotibialis by Hoffmann. Two muscles, four names, two of them shared — which is what Diogo & Molnar mean by false friends.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. Semitendinosus from the ischium to the knee aponeurosis, and semimembranosus — which Hoffmann calls the ischioflexorius, this record's own name — from the pars ascendens ilii and adjacent ischium onto the posterior knee capsule and the posterior proximal head of the tibiofibula. The semimembranosus is divided proximally by a tendinous inscription.

occurrences.name: Flexor tibialis externus + internus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Flexor tibialis externus from the ilioischiadic ligament and flexor tibialis internus from that ligament and the ischial tuberosity, both onto the proximal tibia. Gekko adds a further part to each, the internus tendons meeting at the interarticular area of the knee.

occurrences.name: Flexor tibialis externus + internus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Flexor tibialis internus is FOUR-part here, against three in some Alligator and Caiman latirostris accounts: FTI1 from the postero-lateral ischium to the proximo-medial tibia by a long tendon shared with puboischiotibialis; FTI2 fleshy from the postero-ventral ilium, the largest of the four; FTI3 from the proximo-lateral ischium; FTI4 a small thin muscle from the latero-ventral ilium near the ischium, joining the common tendon. The tibial insertion is the internus'. Flexor tibialis EXTERNUS is named in this record but its insertion is deliberately unscored: it arises by tendon from the postero-lateral ilium and ends, by a long tendon shared with gastrocnemius externus, IN THE PES at the proximal tarsus — not on the tibia.

occurrences.name: M. flexor cruris medialis + flexor cruris lateralis pars pelvica
occurrences.note: = crocodylian flexor tibialis internus 3 and flexor tibialis externus. Crocodylian flexor tibialis internus 1 is LOST between Avialae and Aves — one of the few outright losses in their table.

occurrences.name: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris
occurrences.action: Extend the hip and flex the knee.
occurrences.innervation: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve; the short head of biceps femoris by the common fibular division.

nerves.note: Only the short head of biceps femoris. It is the one hamstring on the dorsal division, which is why the muscle's nerve and its ventral-mass identity disagree here — a real exception, not a scoring error.

occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. The hamstring field, and the origins are what make it one field: biceps femoris from the dorsal ischial tuberosity, semitendinosus from the ischial tuberosity AND the tail — its caudal belly fleshy from the transverse process of caudal vertebra 2 and aponeurotic from C1 and C3 — semimembranosus from the caudal ramus of the ischium. Ercoli et al. read that RESTRICTED caudal origin as a derived mustelid condition, so the row is scored as C1–C3 rather than as a broad caudal sheet. The caudal-vertebral head is the one worth noting — a thigh muscle taking origin from the tail. Insertions run to the tibia in all three, with semimembranosus also on the medial femoral epicondyle and biceps femoris on the lateral.

occurrences.name: Flexor tibialis externus + internus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Hamstrings
occurrences.action: Extend the thigh and flex the knee.
occurrences.innervation: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve; the short head of biceps femoris by the common fibular division.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). All three from the ischial tuberosity, with a second head of biceps femoris from the lateral lip of the linea aspera, to the fibular head and the two tibial condyles. **The group derives from this field and the head-by-head correspondences are not settled** — Diogo & Molnar reject the classical claim of Gregory & Camp, Romer and Haines that the mammalian tenuissimus is the caudal head of biceps femoris, and follow Jones in deriving it from a dorsal tail-region muscle instead. The human row is therefore the mammalian outcome of the split, not a key to it. The short head of biceps femoris has a different nerve from the rest of the muscle it is named part of, which is the sort of thing that makes the split hard to read.

homology.notes: The hamstring group derives from this field, but the correspondences head-by-head are not settled. Diogo & Molnar reject the classical claim (Gregory & Camp 1918; Romer 1922; Haines 1935) that the mammalian tenuissimus is the caudal head of biceps femoris; following Jones (1979) they derive tenuissimus from a dorsal tail-region muscle homologous with the reptilian 'flexor cruris tarsi dorsalis'.

serial.caution: Frequently asserted; the two are innervated by different divisions and derive from opposite masses (hamstrings ventral, triceps dorsal). This correspondence should be treated as functional analogy.

homology.caveat: Leavey et al. (2024), using diceCT on 30 frog species across five locomotor modes, report that bone lengths and pelvic crest sizes are generally NOT reliable predictors of muscle size, and find many-to-one form-function mapping. That is a direct caution against reading muscle proportions off skeletal proportions in fossils, which is the inference osteological correlates are usually recruited for. Correlates locate an attachment; they do not size the muscle that made it.

muscles.name: Gluteus maximus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass.

consensus.origin: Posterior ilium, sacrum, coccyx and sacrotuberous ligament.
consensus.insertion: Gluteal tuberosity of the femur and the iliotibial tract.
consensus.action: Extends and laterally rotates the hip; principal muscle of the erect-posture power stroke.

occurrences.name: Gluteus maximus
occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar note innervation differences between humans and rats: the human gluteus maximus is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve alone, the rat muscle by that nerve plus the inferior branch of the superior gluteal nerve. One of several cases where innervation differs between mammals for muscles otherwise treated as identical.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gluteus superficialis: an aponeurotic head from the iliac crest and fleshy and tendinous fibres from the sacrocaudal aponeurosis over the first two caudal vertebrae, inserting on the lateral greater trochanter and onto the insertions of gluteus medius and tensor fasciae latae.

occurrences.note: The enlargement of this field along the synapsid stem is part of the erect-posture transition documented by Bishop & Pierce.
occurrences.name: Gluteal (dorsal iliac) mass
Gluteus maximus
occurrences.action: Extends and laterally rotates the thigh.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Posterior gluteal line, the posterior sacrum and coccyx and the sacrotuberous ligament; upper fibres to the iliotibial tract, lowermost to the gluteal tuberosity. **The human muscle is what this record is for**, and its name is one of the clearest false friends in Diogo & Molnar's list: the anuran literature applies 'gluteus maximus' to a muscle that is not this one. It is a mammalian differentiation out of the dorsal iliac field, not an inherited muscle, which is why the record has no reptile or bird rows to compare it against.

homology.notes: A mammalian differentiation from the dorsal iliac field. Its name is applied to non-homologous muscles in the anuran literature — one of the clearest cases in Diogo & Molnar's list of false-friend names ('tensor fasciae latae', 'gluteus maximus', 'gemellus', 'obturator externus', 'quadratus femoris', 'obturator internus', 'pectineus', 'adductor longus', 'iliacus', 'sartorius', 'semitendinosus', 'adductor magnus' — none homologous in anurans to the human muscles of the same name).
homology.teaching: The anchor for the false-friend-names lesson. Twelve human muscle names are applied to non-homologous anuran muscles.

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral (flexor) mass of the crus.

consensus.origin: Distal femur, by medial and lateral heads (and from the tibia in some taxa).
consensus.insertion: Calcaneum/fibulare, via the Achilles tendon.
consensus.action: Plantarflexes the ankle; flexes the knee.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius
occurrences.note: Walthall & Ashley-Ross describe no discrete gastrocnemius in Taricha. The flexor primordialis communis occupies the position and takes the femoral epicondylar origin that the amniote gastrocnemius takes, and the paper treats it as one muscle. Recorded here without changing the presence state, since other sources score a gastrocnemius in Caudata; what this source shows is that the boundary between the two is a division that not every author makes.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the ventral proximal tibia and the distal ventral tibial crest, by a broad aponeurosis onto the proximolateral margins of the first three phalanges — not onto a calcaneum, unlike the mammalian condition.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius
occurrences.attachmentNote: Externus arises by a tendon shared with the caudofemoralis longus and from the posterolateral femoral epicondyle, which bears a scattered striated surface; internus from the proximoposterior tibia. Both insert on the calcaneum by a broad tendon.

occurrences.name: M. gastrocnemius
occurrences.note: Ankle plantarflexor.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius
occurrences.action: Plantarflexes the foot; flexes the knee.
occurrences.note: Kardong (2002) derived the mammalian gastrocnemius from the femorotibial ('internal') head; Diogo & Molnar discuss and qualify this.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Lateral head by a strong tendon from the lateral femoral epicondyle and the lateral sesamoid of the knee, medial head from the medial epicondyle, both also from the caudal femoral diaphysis and the knee capsule. Inserts on the caudodorsal calcaneal tubercle, its tendon fusing with those of flexor digitorum superficialis and soleus to form the calcaneal tendon.

occurrences.name: Triceps surae and plantaris
occurrences.action: Plantarflexes the foot; gastrocnemius also flexes the knee.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Gastrocnemius from above the two femoral condyles, soleus from the fibular head and the soleal line of the tibia, plantaris from above the lateral condyle, all to the dorsum of the calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon. **Femoral and tibial origins at once**, which is what this record says varies: head count and the femoral-versus-tibial origin are the two variables across Tetrapoda, and a human has both states in one muscle group. In anurans the same muscle is the principal jump-propulsion muscle and is hypertrophied past everything else in the leg.

homology.notes: Universal across Tetrapoda. Head count and the femoral versus tibial origin vary. In anurans it is the principal jump-propulsion muscle and is hypertrophied relative to every other muscle of the leg.

serial.caution: The crural and antebrachial flexor masses correspond as fields, but muscle-for-muscle mapping within them is unreliable.

muscles.name: Tibialis anterior
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) mass of the crus.

consensus.origin: Proximal tibia and the interosseous membrane.
consensus.insertion: Medial tarsals and the base of metatarsal I.
consensus.action: Dorsiflexes the ankle; inverts the foot.

occurrences.name: Extensor cruris tibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. extensor cruris tibialis. Visible from both ventral and dorsal views as it fans from the femoral epicondyle across the anterior face of the tibia — three rows for one muscle on one bone, because it wraps.
occurrences.origin: Tibial (medial) epicondyle of the femur.
occurrences.insertion: Extensively on the anterodorsal and anteroventral faces of the tibia.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the entire anterior surface of the tibia, tendinously onto digit I. In Gekko the tendon also contributes to the lateral digital tendon.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the proximomedial tibia to the dorsolateral proximal metatarsals I-II; the metatarsal bases carry coarse rugosities marking the insertion.

occurrences.name: Tibialis cranialis (classical) / extensor digitorum longus (Hattori & Tsuihiji 2021)
occurrences.note: Which avian muscle this record corresponds to is exactly what Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) dispute. Scored uncertain rather than picking a side.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.action: Dorsiflexes and inverts the foot.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tibialis cranialis from the craniolateral proximal quarter of the tibia including the lateral condyle and the lateral margin of the cnemial crest, from the proximal interosseous membrane, and by a second tendinous head from the cranial head of the fibula. Inserts on the medial aspect of the ventral tubercle at the base of metatarsal I.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. The insertion tendon additionally contributes to the lateral digital tendon, which Eublepharis's does not.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.origin: Broad area on the shaft of the tibia — the proximal two-thirds of the dorsal surface and the distal two-thirds of the ventral aspect.
occurrences.insertion: Medial margin of metatarsal I.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana. The two squamates differ here and the difference is scored rather than averaged: the iguana's dorsal origin stops short of the distal tibia and the monitor's does not.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.origin: Broad area on the shaft of the tibia, the dorsal surface origin continuing to the distal end of the bone.
occurrences.insertion: Medial margin of metatarsal I.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus indicus. Against Iguana, the dorsal origin runs the whole length of the tibia.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.origin: Dorsomedial margin of the tibia, marked on the bone by a rugose longitudinal sulcus.
occurrences.insertion: Proximomedial end of metatarsal I, marked by a tubercle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Chelydra serpentina. Both ends leave a correlate — a sulcus at the origin and a tubercle at the insertion — which is what makes this muscle reconstructable in a fossil turtle.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.origin: Proximal-most portion of the dorsal aspect of the tibia, marked with surface rugosity that broadens proximodistally on the lateral side.
occurrences.insertion: Bulge on the dorsal aspect of each of metatarsals I and II.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Paleosuchus palpebrosus.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.origin: Proximal-most portion of the dorsal aspect of the tibia, marked by distinct rugosity.
occurrences.insertion: Bulge on the dorsal aspect of each of metatarsals I and II.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Broad surface between the cranial and lateral cnemial crests and the dorsolateral aspect of the tibial shaft, tapering distally.
occurrences.insertion: Processes on the proximodorsal lips of the phalanges of digits II-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus gallus. The other half of the revision: Hattori & Tsuihiji put the avian m. extensor digitorum longus HERE, with the non-avian tibialis anterior, on the strength of the shared tibial origin. Note what that does to the shared cnemial crests — under their scheme both anterior tibial muscles take them in birds, the tibialis cranialis on the crests' expansions and this one on the surface between them.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Broad surface between the cranial and lateral cnemial crests and the dorsolateral tibial shaft.
occurrences.insertion: Processes on the proximodorsal lips of the phalanges of digits II-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Grus japonensis. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.action: Dorsiflexes and inverts the foot.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lateral tibial condyle and the upper lateral tibial surface to the medial cuneiform and the first metatarsal — the preaxial dorsiflexor, unchanged in position from the amphibian extensor cruris tibialis and reaching the same first-digit side of the foot. The medial cuneiform is scored as `distal-tarsals`.

homology.notes: Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) propose that the classical homologies of the two anterior tibial muscles are swapped: on their reading the avian m. tibialis cranialis is homologous with the NON-AVIAN m. extensor digitorum longus, and the avian m. extensor digitorum longus with the non-avian m. tibialis anterior. Their argument is that this requires no drastic change in attachment sites between avian and non-avian homologues, whereas the classical scheme does. The classical scheme descends from Romer (1923-27) and, they note, had been used uncritically by palaeontologists for a century. Their method weights morphological and functional congruence over innervation, on the grounds that nerve-muscle specificity is itself variable across taxa — which is the reverse of the priority used elsewhere in this dataset, and worth noting as a genuine methodological disagreement rather than a detail. Allen et al. (2021) independently adopt the revised scheme in their crocodylian-to-avian homology table, equating the crocodylian extensor digitorum longus with the avian m. tibialis cranialis. That is a second line of support for Hattori & Tsuihiji's reading against the classical one, from authors working on moment arms rather than on homology, so the agreement is not circular.
homology.openQuestion: Is the avian tibialis cranialis the homologue of the non-avian tibialis anterior (Romer's scheme, followed by most of the literature) or of the non-avian extensor digitorum longus (Hattori & Tsuihiji 2021)? The two schemes imply different attachment histories across the archosaur stem, so fossil muscle reconstruction in theropods depends on which is right.

muscles.name: Extensor digitorum longus (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass of the crus.

consensus.origin: Lateral tibial condyle, proximal fibula and the interosseous membrane.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal aponeuroses of the digits.
consensus.action: Extends the toes; dorsiflexes the ankle.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thin, lying on the dorsal crus between the extensor tarsi tibialis and the extensor cruris et tarsi fibularis. Unlike its forelimb counterpart it stops at the metatarsals rather than reaching the phalanges.
occurrences.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the femur, anterior to the extensor cruris et tarsi fibularis; sometimes a few fibres from the tibial spine.
occurrences.insertion: Bases of the metatarsals, by many small tendons.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: From the lateral femoral extensor fossa and condyle to the proximodorsal metatarsals III-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the lateral femoral extensor fossa and lateral condyle onto the proximodorsal metatarsals III-IV, which bear a smooth bump at the insertion. Note that this is a femoral origin, not a tibial one — relevant to the Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) dispute over which anterior tibial muscle is which.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: See the tibialis anterior record: which avian muscle is the homologue is disputed.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: In humans the fibularis tertius derives from the extensor digitorum longus anlage (Lewis 1910). In rats the fibularis digiti quinti derives from the extensor digiti quinti anlage. The two are therefore NOT homologous, despite both being called a 'fibularis' and both being innervated by the deep fibular nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Femoral, not tibial, in origin — from the lateral condyle of the femur and the aponeurosis over tibialis cranialis — so it crosses the knee as well as the ankle. Four flat tendons to the distal phalanges of digits II–V, fused en route with the tendons of extensor digitorum brevis and, on digit V, extensor digitorum lateralis.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Dorsomedial aspect of the lateral distal condyle of the femur.
occurrences.insertion: Metatarsals II and III by two tendons, each passing the lateral aspect of the proximal shaft to the tubercle on its lateroplantar aspect.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana. This is the muscle Hattori & Tsuihiji standardise as m. tibialis cranialis, and its avian member is the point of the paper: on their reading the bird's m. tibialis cranialis belongs on THIS record and not on `tibialis-anterior`, where the classical scheme puts it.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Dorsomedial aspect of the lateral distal condyle of the femur.
occurrences.insertion: Metatarsals II and III by two tendons, onto the tubercle on the lateroplantar aspect of each proximal shaft.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus indicus. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal aspect of the lateral distal condyle of the femur.
occurrences.insertion: Lateral sides of metatarsals I-IV and the proximodorsal lip of phalanx I-2.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Chelydra serpentina. The widest insertion of any sauropsid on this record — all four metatarsals — and turtles vary in it: Gadow (1882) put the insertion on the proximal phalanges of digits I-IV instead, and Ribbing (1938) found the Emys condition scored here. This is the muscle Hattori & Tsuihiji standardise as m. tibialis cranialis, and its avian member is the point of the paper: on their reading the bird's m. tibialis cranialis belongs on THIS record and not on `tibialis-anterior`, where the classical scheme puts it.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Dorsal aspect of the femur just proximal to the lateral distal condyle.
occurrences.insertion: Tubercle on the medial margin of the proximal shaft of each of metatarsals II-IV, merging at the medial-most site with the tibialis anterior.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Paleosuchus palpebrosus. An MT I insertion is reported by Gadow (1882), Ribbing (1909, 1938) and Cong et al. (1998) and was not found here. This is the muscle Hattori & Tsuihiji standardise as m. tibialis cranialis, and its avian member is the point of the paper: on their reading the bird's m. tibialis cranialis belongs on THIS record and not on `tibialis-anterior`, where the classical scheme puts it.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Dorsal aspect of the femur just proximal to the lateral distal condyle.
occurrences.insertion: Tubercle on the medial margin of the proximal shaft of each of metatarsals II-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Tibialis cranialis
occurrences.origin: Distal extremity of the lateral distal condyle of the femur, at the fovea tendinis m. tibialis cranialis, plus the lateral expansion of the cranial cnemial crest and the dorsoventral expansion of the lateral cnemial crest of the tibia.
occurrences.insertion: Tubercles on the dorsal aspect of the proximal tarsometatarsus — the tuberositas m. tibialis cranialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus gallus. **The row the homology revision turns on.** Hattori & Tsuihiji place the avian m. tibialis cranialis here, with the non-avian extensor digitorum longus, because the femoral origin is conserved across all four clades and the avian tuberositas on the tarsometatarsus sits where metatarsals II and III would have been. The classical scheme instead pairs it with `tibialis-anterior`, which requires the extensor digitorum longus origin to cross the knee joint and the tibialis cranialis to lose its MT I insertion. The tibial origin, on the two cnemial crests, is the avian addition. Two of the fifteen orphan correlates in GAPS §3 close on this row.

occurrences.name: Tibialis cranialis
