occurrences.origin: Distal extremity of the lateral distal condyle of the femur and the cranial and lateral cnemial crests of the tibia.
occurrences.insertion: Tubercles on the dorsal aspect of the proximal tarsometatarsus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Grus japonensis. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus
occurrences.action: Extend the toes and dorsiflex the foot.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Extensor digitorum longus from the lateral tibial condyle, the anterior fibula and the interosseous membrane to the extensor expansions of the lateral four toes; extensor hallucis longus from the middle fibula to the distal phalanx of the hallux. **Fibularis tertius is scored here as a disputed part rather than with the fibularis group**, and the reason is its nerve: Diogo & Molnar make the point that fibularis tertius and fibularis digiti quinti are supplied by the DEEP fibular nerve, with the extensors, not by the superficial fibular nerve that supplies the true fibularis muscles. The name groups it with the peronei; the innervation groups it here.

homology.notes: The muscle itself is straightforward; the interest is in its derivatives. The human fibularis tertius / rat fibularis digiti quinti case is one of Diogo & Molnar's cleanest demonstrations that shared name plus shared nerve still does not establish homology. Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) propose that the classical homologies of the two anterior tibial muscles are swapped: on their reading the avian m. tibialis cranialis is homologous with the NON-AVIAN m. extensor digitorum longus, and the avian m. extensor digitorum longus with the non-avian m. tibialis anterior. Their argument is that this requires no drastic change in attachment sites between avian and non-avian homologues, whereas the classical scheme does. The classical scheme descends from Romer (1923-27) and, they note, had been used uncritically by palaeontologists for a century. Their method weights morphological and functional congruence over innervation, on the grounds that nerve-muscle specificity is itself variable across taxa — which is the reverse of the priority used elsewhere in this dataset, and worth noting as a genuine methodological disagreement rather than a detail. Allen et al. (2021) independently adopt the revised scheme in their crocodylian-to-avian homology table, equating the crocodylian extensor digitorum longus with the avian m. tibialis cranialis. That is a second line of support for Hattori & Tsuihiji's reading against the classical one, from authors working on moment arms rather than on homology, so the agreement is not circular.

serial.note: In rats, the short extensors of digits 2 and 3 are fused in BOTH limbs — extensor indicis in the forelimb, extensor digitorum brevis in the hindlimb. Diogo & Molnar show these fusions are independently derived, producing apparent serial similarity by parallelism.

homology.teaching: The rat double-fusion case is the single most economical illustration of parallelism masquerading as serial homology.

muscles.name: Fibularis (peroneus) group
muscles.developmental: Somitic; lateral compartment of the crus, dorsal mass.
synonyms: peroneus longus / brevis / tertius / digiti quinti

consensus.insertion: Metatarsals and lateral tarsals.
consensus.action: Everts the foot; plantarflexes (longus, brevis) or dorsiflexes (tertius).
consensus.innervation: Superficial fibular nerve (longus, brevis); deep fibular nerve (tertius, digiti quinti).

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus + brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. M. peroneus, partly tendinous proximally and partly muscular from almost the whole fibula, onto the fifth metatarsal. Gekko has two slips.

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus + brevis
occurrences.note: Both insert on the anterior surface of metatarsal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fibularis longus arises on the fibular shaft distal to the iliofibular tubercle; brevis from the distal fibular shaft and the anterior tibial aponeurosis. Both insert on the anterior surface of metatarsal V.

occurrences.name: M. fibularis longus + brevis
occurrences.note: Names retained; longus plantarflexes, brevis dorsiflexes.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus, brevis (+ tertius in humans, digiti quinti in rats)
occurrences.action: Evert the foot; the longus also supports the transverse arch.
occurrences.innervation: Superficial fibular nerve for longus and brevis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Fibularis brevis from the anterolateral and caudolateral surfaces of the middle of the fibula in two bellies, inserting on the dorsolateral tubercle of metatarsal V. Fibularis longus is the reason for the tibial and calcaneal rows: it arises tendinously from the CRANIAL HEAD OF THE FIBULA *and* from the lateral aspect of the LATERAL CONDYLE OF THE TIBIA with the adjacent tibial diaphysis, and it reaches a first insertion on the laterodistal CALCANEUS and the proximal margin of the metatarsal V tubercle before running internal to the long plantar ligament to a final attachment on the lateral surface of the plantar tubercle of metatarsal I. Both round the lateral malleolus. The tibial origin and the calcaneal insertion were missing while this note claimed the only omission was that the fibular fields were finer than one row could carry — a whole bone at each end, not a matter of granularity.

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus + brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Peroneus longus + peroneus brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus from the lateral femoral epicondyle just distal to the flexor digitorum longus origin; brevis from almost the entire anterior, lateral and medial surfaces of the fibula, over nearly its whole length.
occurrences.insertion: Longus into a depression on the dorsolateral aspect of the shaft of metatarsal V; brevis onto the outer process on the proximolateral margin of metatarsal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana. The longus insertion is a depression, against the 'lateral plantar tubercle' of Russell & Bauer (2008) — Hattori & Tsuihiji contradict them on the correlate itself, not on the muscle.

occurrences.name: Peroneus longus + peroneus brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus from the lateral femoral epicondyle; brevis from almost the whole fibula.
occurrences.insertion: Longus into a depression on the dorsolateral shaft of metatarsal V; brevis onto the proximolateral margin of metatarsal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus indicus. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Peroneus anterior + peroneus brevis
occurrences.origin: Peroneus anterior — the longus of this record — from the distal half of the dorsal aspect of the fibula, the origin marked by a slightly excavated surface; brevis from the distal end of the fibula.
occurrences.insertion: Peroneus anterior onto the dorsal aspect of the proximolateral margins of metatarsal V and phalanx IV-1; brevis onto the proximal margin of the dorsal aspect of metatarsal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Chelydra serpentina. The femoral origin the squamates give the longus is gone here — both heads are on the fibula, which is the condition crocodilians share and which Hattori & Tsuihiji use to group the two clades against lepidosaurs and birds.

occurrences.name: Peroneus longus + peroneus brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus from almost the entire laterodorsal aspect of the fibula, the surface between the longitudinal ridges on its dorsal and lateral aspects; brevis from the flat laterodorsal surface of the distal two-thirds of the fibular shaft.
occurrences.insertion: Longus merges with the brevis and inserts on the flat surface at its insertion site; brevis on the proximolateral margin of metatarsal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Paleosuchus palpebrosus. Both origins are bounded by ridges or are flat surfaces, so the fibula records the whole group.

occurrences.name: Peroneus longus + peroneus brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus from almost the entire laterodorsal aspect of the fibula; brevis from the laterodorsal aspect of the distal two-thirds of the fibular shaft.
occurrences.insertion: Longus onto the brevis insertion; brevis on the proximolateral margin of metatarsal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus + fibularis brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus from the proximal margins of the cranial and lateral cnemial crests, the patellar tendon and associated fascia; brevis from most of the interosseal space between tibia and fibula — a narrow surface between two longitudinal ridges on the distal two-thirds of the tibial shaft, and the dorsal surface of the distal half of the fibula.
occurrences.insertion: Longus onto soft tissue, the sustentaculum tarsi and the insertion tendon of the flexor perforatus digiti III; brevis onto a proximal surface near the lateral margin of the hypotarsus, the tuberculum m. fibularis brevis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus gallus. **The insertion is different because the bone is gone.** In all three non-avian clades both heads end on metatarsal V; birds have lost it, and Hattori & Tsuihiji read the avian insertions — on the hypotarsus, on soft tissue and on another muscle's tendon — as the consequence. An attachment relocating because its element was lost, which is the same case as the therian supracoracoideus and the coracoid. The longus account is Fujioka's (1962) on Gallus rather than their own dissection.

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus + fibularis brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus from the proximal cnemial crests and the patellar tendon; brevis from the interosseal space between tibia and fibula.
occurrences.insertion: Longus onto soft tissue, the sustentaculum tarsi and the flexor perforatus digiti III tendon; brevis near the lateral margin of the hypotarsus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Grus japonensis. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus and brevis
occurrences.action: Evert the foot and assist plantarflexion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Longus from the upper two-thirds of the lateral fibula, crossing the sole deep to the intrinsic muscles to reach the medial cuneiform and the first metatarsal; brevis from the lower third to the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal. **Only the two superficial-fibular muscles are scored on this record.** Fibularis tertius carries the group's name and the extensors' nerve, and is scored with `extensor-digitorum-longus-hl` instead — this record's assessment already says the innervation cuts against the obvious grouping, and this is what acting on that looks like. Note also the longus tendon: it crosses the whole sole transversely, so a lateral muscle ends on the medial side of the foot.

homology.notes: Diogo & Molnar dwell on this group because the innervation is diagnostic and cuts against the obvious grouping. The fibularis tertius and fibularis digiti quinti are innervated by the DEEP fibular nerve — which supplies short extensors such as extensor digitorum brevis — not by the superficial fibular nerve that supplies the true lateral muscles fibularis longus and brevis. Deriving them from the lateral mass would require the innervation to have changed; deriving them from the extensor anlage does not.
homology.openQuestion: Diogo & Molnar state explicitly that a firm answer requires a much more extensive analysis including innervation and developmental data.
homology.teaching: Innervation as a decisive argument. Two muscles sit in the lateral compartment and carry a lateral-compartment name, but their nerve says they belong to the extensor group.

muscles.name: Popliteus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; derived from the interosseus cruris.

consensus.insertion: Posterior proximal tibia.
consensus.action: Unlocks the extended knee by rotating the tibia; medially rotates the leg.

occurrences.name: Popliteus
occurrences.attachmentNote: By a thick short tendon from the lateral femoral condyle and the aponeurosis over the distal lateral femur, to the medial and caudal aspects of the proximal two-thirds of the tibia. Some fibres insert onto flexor digitorum medialis rather than bone.

occurrences.name: Interosseus cruris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Scored from Zaaf et al.'s M. popliteus: from the proximal fibula, partly muscular and partly tendinous onto the anterolateral tibial shaft. This record's Lepidosauria occurrence is named 'interosseus cruris', the name Abdala & Diogo use for the same tibiofibular muscle.

occurrences.name: Interosseus cruris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Popliteus
occurrences.action: Unlocks the extended knee by laterally rotating the femur on the tibia.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lateral femoral condyle to the posterior tibia above the soleal line. **A muscle that has moved to the other end of a bone.** Its ancestor is the interosseus cruris, a muscle running between tibia and fibula in the position an amniote fills with the interosseous membrane; the popliteus has left the fibula and climbed onto the femur, converting a leg muscle into a knee muscle. That is why `interosseus-cruris` is scored absent in a human on the next record and this one is present.

homology.notes: The popliteus derives from the interosseus cruris.

serial.caution: This is Diogo & Molnar's headline counter-example. The popliteus and pronator teres are frequently listed as forelimb–hindlimb topological equivalents, but they derive from DIFFERENT anlagen: popliteus from the interosseus cruris, pronator teres from the flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis. The true ontogenetic counterparts are hindlimb tibialis posterior and forelimb palmaris profundus / pronator profundus.

homology.teaching: The cleanest single case for separating topological correspondence from developmental correspondence. Worth teaching verbatim.

muscles.name: Tibialis posterior
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral mass of the crus.

consensus.origin: Interosseous membrane and the adjacent tibia and fibula.
consensus.insertion: Navicular, cuneiforms and the bases of the middle metatarsals.
consensus.action: Inverts the foot; plantarflexes the ankle; supports the medial longitudinal arch.

occurrences.name: Tibialis posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tibialis caudalis from the caudal tibial shaft and the cranial, medial and caudal aspects of the fibular head, through the sulcus of the medial malleolus, to the medial and ventral surfaces of the centrale and tarsal I and to the sesamoid between them.

occurrences.name: Tibialis posterior
occurrences.action: Inverts the foot and assists plantarflexion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Interosseous membrane and the facing surfaces of both leg bones, to the navicular tuberosity, the medial cuneiform and metatarsals 2-4 — the widest tarsal insertion of any muscle in the human foot, and the main dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch.

serial.note: Diogo & Molnar identify hindlimb tibialis posterior and forelimb palmaris profundus / pronator profundus (pronator quadratus) as the REAL ontogenetic counterparts — as against the popliteus/pronator teres pairing, which is topological only.

homology.teaching: The positive half of the popliteus lesson: this is what a developmentally supported correspondence looks like.

muscles.name: Flexor digitorum longus (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass of the crus.

consensus.insertion: Plantar surfaces of the distal phalanges.
consensus.action: Flexes the toes; plantarflexes the ankle.

occurrences.name: Flexor primordialis communis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. flexor primordialis communis. Five tendons, against four in the hand — the pes retains digit V. Its function is given as pressing the sole against the ground rather than flexing the digits.
occurrences.origin: Chiefly the posteroventral face of the fibula, with part arising by tendon from the fibular epicondyle of the femur.
occurrences.insertion: Plantar aponeurosis, which divides into five tendons to the proximal end of the terminal phalanx of each digit.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the lateral femoral epicondyle; distally a stout tendon serving digits I-IV. Ankle plantarflexor, active in stance.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: Femoral origin; inserts on the proximoventral unguals I-III.
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the ventral distal femur and lateral condyle, which carries parallel striae aligned with the femoral long axis, onto the proximoventral unguals I-III.

occurrences.name: M. flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: Together with the flexor hallucis longus, forms the tendon system that produces automatic toe flexion when the ankle flexes — the mechanism of perching. Ankle plantarflexor.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Flexor digitorum medialis from the caudal and caudomedial aspects of the fibular head, through the sulcus of the medial malleolus. It fuses with flexor digitorum lateralis at the distal tarsals into a tendinous sheet that divides into five tendons, which pass through the rings formed by flexor digitorum brevis and insert on the distal phalanges.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus
occurrences.action: Flex the toes and assist plantarflexion of the foot.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Flexor digitorum longus from the middle half of the posterior tibia to the distal phalanges of digits 2-5; flexor hallucis longus from the lower two-thirds of the posterior fibula to the distal phalanx of the hallux. **The hand and the foot went opposite ways here.** In the hand the long flexor split into a superficial and a deep layer inserting at two levels on the same digits; in the foot it split by digit instead, one muscle for the hallux and one for the rest, both reaching the terminal phalanges as the ancestral single plate did. Compare the `flexor-digitorum-longus` human row.

serial.note: Among the strongest forelimb–hindlimb correspondences. Diogo & Molnar's Fig. 3 shows that the distal (zeugopodial and autopodial) muscles of the salamander fore and hind limbs are strikingly similar, while the proximal (girdle and stylopodial) muscles are clearly different.

homology.teaching: The distal-greater-than-proximal similarity gradient is visible in a single salamander dissection.

muscles.name: Flexores breves superficiales (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Middle phalanges.
consensus.action: Flexes the toes at the metatarsophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tripartite for every digit except the first, which lacks the phalangeal connection. The manus counterpart differs: there the slips flank the metacarpals of digits II and III but not I and IV.
occurrences.origin: Dorsal side of the plantar fascia.
occurrences.insertion: For digits II-V, the ventral side of the distal ends of the metatarsals and the ventral surface of the proximal end of the proximal phalanx; for digit I, the distal end of the metatarsal only.

occurrences.name: Mm. flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.note: A single muscular body in Triprion despite the plural name, on the lateroplantar tarsus beneath the aponeurosis plantaris.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Despite the plural name, a single muscular body in Triprion, on the lateroplantar tarsal surface and ventrally concealed by the aponeurosis plantaris.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Flexor digitorum brevis of the pes, from the proximal extremity of the fifth metatarsal onto the terminal phalanx. Gekko differs digit by digit, inserting at the distal end of metatarsal I on digit I, of the second phalanx on III and IV, and of the first phalanx on II and V.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum brevis superficialis
occurrences.note: Layer 1 of the seven-layer pedal scheme.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Flexor digitorum brevis superficialis, digits I-IV, from the ventral calcaneum with digit-specific variation. Layer 1 of the seven-layer pedal scheme Pereyra et al. set out.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Flexor digitorum brevis, taking origin by an aponeurosis from the insertion of the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon at the plantar surface of the calcaneal tubercle. Its tendons split around those of flexor digitorum profundus, forming the rings the deep tendons pass through, and insert on the plantar and proximal aspects of the middle phalanges of II–V and the proximal phalanx of digit I.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Digit by digit: the distal end of metatarsal I for digit I, of the second phalanx for III and IV, and of the first phalanx for II and V — where Eublepharis inserts on the terminal phalanx throughout.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum brevis
occurrences.action: Flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints of digits 2-5.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Calcaneal tuberosity, plantar aponeurosis and intermuscular septa, to the bases of the middle phalanges of digits 2-5, splitting to let the long flexor tendons through. **The split tendon is inherited, not invented.** The same bifurcation is described for crocodylians, lepidosaurs and turtles in the hand, where the short flexor tendons divide to pass the long flexor, and Burch reconstructs it for *Tawa*. Humans kept it in the foot and lost the layer in the hand — see the `flexores-breves-superficiales` row, scored uncertain there for exactly that reason.

serial.note: Part of the strongly corresponding distal muscle set.

muscles.name: Contrahentes digitorum (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Proximal phalanges.
consensus.action: Adducts the toes toward the foot's axis.

occurrences.name: Contrahentes digitorum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Passes from the tarsals along the ventral axis of the metatarsals. As in the hand, part of the origin is on the caput longum tendon rather than on bone.
occurrences.origin: The flat tendon of the caput longum musculorum contrahentium, and the tarsal bones.
occurrences.insertion: Proximal phalanx of each digit.

occurrences.name: Mm. contrahentes digitorum pedis
occurrences.note: Blotto et al. (2020) record a full contrahens series in the anuran foot, including one serving the prehallux — the pedal counterpart of the prepollex contrahens in the hand.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Blotto et al. record a full contrahens series in the anuran foot, including one serving the prehallux.

occurrences.name: Interdigiti dorsales + ventrales
occurrences.note: Running between successive metatarsals.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The interdigiti dorsales and ventrales of Pereyra et al., running between successive metatarsals; their origins are marked by longitudinally oriented fine striae on the proximolateral metatarsal surfaces.

occurrences.name: Adductor hallucis
occurrences.note: As in the hand, the contrahens layer is largely lost in mammals, with the adductor hallucis surviving as its principal representative.

occurrences.name: Adductor hallucis
occurrences.action: Adducts the great toe.
occurrences.innervation: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Oblique head from the bases of metatarsals 2-4, transverse head from the heads of metatarsals 3-5, both to the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the hallux. **The foot and the hand each kept exactly one contrahens, and it is the one to digit I in both.** Adductor hallucis here, adductor pollicis on `contrahentes-digitorum` — two limbs, the same survivor, the same two-headed arrangement, in an animal that uses the two limbs for completely different things.

muscles.name: Flexores breves profundi (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deepest ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Proximal phalanges and metatarsophalangeal sesamoids.
consensus.action: Flexes the metatarsophalangeal joints; abducts and adducts the toes.

occurrences.name: Mm. flexores breves profundi
occurrences.note: Includes slips serving the prehallux.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum brevis profundus
occurrences.note: Deep flexor layer; metatarsal origins marked by fine striae.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Flexor digitorum brevis profundus, digits I-IV, from metatarsals I-III and V and the distal calcaneum. The metatarsal origins are marked by fine striae — the pedal correlates Pereyra et al. identify for the first time.

occurrences.name: Interossei (plantar and dorsal)
occurrences.innervation: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve.

occurrences.name: Interossei and the short flexors of the hallux and fifth digit
occurrences.action: Flex the metatarsophalangeal joints; the interossei abduct and adduct the digits about the axis of digit II.
occurrences.innervation: Lateral plantar nerve, deep branch; flexor hallucis brevis by the medial plantar nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Four dorsal interossei from adjacent metatarsal shafts, three plantar interossei from the bases and medial sides of metatarsals 3-5, flexor hallucis brevis from the cuboid and lateral cuneiform, flexor digiti minimi brevis from the base of metatarsal V. **Scored on this record's own mammalian synonymy**, which names the interossei plantares and dorsales as its mammalian representatives. The same carve-up is contested in the hand and is handled the same way there. Note the axis: the human hand abducts about digit III and the foot about digit II, so the two sets of interossei are arranged around different rays.

serial.note: One of the strongest distal correspondences: the same three-layer plantar/palmar system in both limbs.

muscles.name: Pubotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral (flexor) muscle mass of the hindlimb bud.

consensus.origin: Anterior edge and anterior ventral face of the pelvis.
consensus.insertion: Anterior face of the proximal tibia.
consensus.action: Supports the body during walking and flexes the knee.
consensus.innervation: Ventral division of the lumbosacral plexus.

occurrences.name: Pubotibialis
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Its parallel fibres pass anterior to the puboischiotibialis to a proximal tibial insertion. Function attributed on the strength of Ashley-Ross (1995) electromyography in Dicamptodon, not inferred from geometry.

homology.notes: A pelvis-to-tibia muscle anterior to the puboischiotibialis. Its relation to the amniote ambiens is not established here.

muscles.name: Femorofibularis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral (flexor) muscle mass of the hindlimb bud.

consensus.origin: Ventral face of the distal end of the femur.
consensus.insertion: Posterolateral face of the fibula.
consensus.action: Flexes the knee.
consensus.innervation: Ventral division of the lumbosacral plexus; branches of the same nerve serve the distal ischioflexorius.

occurrences.name: Femorofibularis
occurrences.note: Robust in Taricha, against the thin narrow muscle usual in salamanders. Ashley-Ross (1992) found a size trade-off with the ischioflexorius: Dicamptodon and newly metamorphosed Ambystoma have a large ischioflexorius and a slender femorofibularis, older Ambystoma the reverse, and Darevsky & Salomatina (1989) report the same trade-off in Paramesotriton. Francis (1934) noted that branches of one nerve supply the distal ischioflexorius and the femorofibularis, which is the basis for treating them as alternative solutions to one mechanical demand. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: A short femur-to-fibula strap crossing only the knee, against the ischioflexorius which runs from the pelvis to the sole. Two muscles of very different span substituting for one another in size is a caution against reading function from length.

homology.teaching: A reciprocal size relationship between two muscles that share a nerve branch but not a span. The trade-off shows up across species and within one species across ontogeny.
homology.notes: No amniote counterpart is established. Shared innervation with the distal ischioflexorius is the strongest evidence bearing on its identity.

muscles.name: Caudalipuboischiotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; caudal hypaxial series recruited to the hindlimb.

consensus.origin: Transverse process of the fourth caudal vertebra.
consensus.insertion: The tendinous inscription dividing the puboischiotibialis.
consensus.action: Assists the puboischiotibialis in limb retraction and flexes the tail laterally.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the anterior caudal spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Caudalipuboischiotibialis
occurrences.note: Coactive with the puboischiotibialis during walking (Ashley-Ross 1995). Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: A muscle with a skeletal origin and no skeletal insertion: it ends on another muscle's tendinous inscription. Salamandra and Cryptobranchus lack that inscription altogether, so in those genera the insertion has nothing to attach to.

homology.notes: One of three tail-to-pelvis muscles. Its insertion on a tendinous inscription rather than bone means it cannot be reconstructed from a skeleton.

muscles.name: Iliocaudalis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; caudal epaxial series reaching the pelvic girdle.

consensus.insertion: Ilium.
consensus.action: Draws the tail laterally.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the anterior caudal spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Iliocaudalis
occurrences.note: Its fibres run parallel to the epaxial muscles and it is distinguishable from them only by its insertion. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: A muscle identified by where it ends rather than by any visible boundary — the clearest case in this source of an attachment doing the work of delimiting a muscle.

occurrences.name: Iliococcygeus
occurrences.action: Supports the pelvic viscera; draws the coccyx forward.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The human pelvic floor is tail musculature that stayed behind.** Iliococcygeus is one of the three parts of levator ani, running from the tendinous arch over the obturator internus fascia to the coccyx and the anococcygeal body. In a lizard the same muscle moves the tail; in an animal whose tail is a coccyx it has become a sling supporting the viscera, without changing either attachment in kind. Gest also lists pubococcygeus, puborectalis, pubovaginalis and levator prostatae, which are the pubic-origin members of the same sheet.

homology.teaching: Where a muscle has no visible border with its neighbours, its insertion is the only thing that makes it a muscle at all.

muscles.name: Ischiocaudalis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; caudal hypaxial series reaching the pelvic girdle.

consensus.origin: Transverse process of the fourth caudal vertebra.
consensus.insertion: Posterior border of the ischium.
consensus.action: Draws the tail laterally.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the anterior caudal spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Ischiocaudalis
occurrences.note: The most medial of the three ventral muscles connecting tail and pelvic girdle. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Flat, thin and strap-like. With the caudalipuboischiotibialis and caudofemoralis it forms a series of three, all from the anterior caudal transverse processes, differing in where they end.

occurrences.name: Coccygeus
occurrences.action: Supports the pelvic viscera; draws the coccyx forward.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Ischial spine to the lateral coccyx and the lowest sacrum — the ischiococcygeus under its clinical name. With [[iliocaudalis]] it is the second half of the answer to what happened to the caudal musculature in an animal with no tail: it did not disappear, it took over the pelvic outlet.

muscles.name: Extensor tarsi tibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) muscle mass of the hindlimb bud.

consensus.insertion: Ventral surface of the tibiale.
consensus.action: Supinates the foot.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal division of the lumbosacral plexus.

occurrences.name: Extensor tarsi tibialis
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crosses knee and ankle to reach a proximal tarsal. Function presumed from geometry, not measured.

muscles.name: Extensor cruris et tarsi fibularis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) muscle mass of the hindlimb bud.

consensus.insertion: Posterodorsal and posteroventral faces of the fibula, with a portion on the fibulare.
consensus.action: Extends the knee.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal division of the lumbosacral plexus.

occurrences.name: Extensor cruris et tarsi fibularis
occurrences.note: The postaxial complement of the extensor cruris tibialis: the two wrap the tibia and fibula respectively from the two femoral epicondyles. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Three rows on two bones for one muscle, because it wraps the fibula from dorsal to ventral and continues onto the proximal tarsus.

muscles.name: Interosseus cruris
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep layer between the zeugopodial elements.

consensus.insertion: Distal portion of the tibia.
consensus.action: Stabilises the two long bones of the crus against one another.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal division of the lumbosacral plexus.

occurrences.name: Interosseus cruris
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Joins the medial sides of tibia and fibula. Its serial counterpart in the forelimb is the pronator profundus, which in salamanders runs the other way — from the ulna across to the radial side — and acts as a pronator rather than a strut.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed, and the structure in its position is the interosseous membrane — a ligament where a salamander has a muscle. It is not simply lost: the popliteus derives from it, and is scored on that record. One ancestral muscle here becomes a ligament and a knee rotator in the same animal.

homology.notes: Occupies the position of the amniote interosseous membrane as a muscle rather than a ligament.

muscles.name: Pronator profundus (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Lateral face of the distal tibia, the tibiale, and the base of the first metatarsal.
consensus.action: Pronates the foot.

occurrences.name: Pronator profundus
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Roughly triangular, converging from the postaxial to the preaxial side of the ankle — the same crossing course as its counterpart in the hand.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed. The human leg has no pronator: the tibia and fibula do not rotate on each other the way the radius and ulna do, and the interosseous membrane between them is a strut rather than an axis. Compare the forearm, where three separate pronators and a supinator are scored.

homology.notes: Walthall & Ashley-Ross give the same name to this muscle and to its counterpart in the hand, which is why the two are separate records here.

muscles.name: Contrahentium caput longum (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: A flat tendon attaching to the distal tarsal bones.
consensus.action: Flexes the tarsus.

occurrences.name: Caput longum musculorum contrahentium
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thin, lying deep to the plantar fascia. Its insertion tendon is in turn the origin of the contrahentes digitorum, the same chained arrangement the hand shows.

occurrences.name: Contrahentium caput longum
occurrences.attachmentNote: A single muscle from the medial ligamentum calcanei, inserting fleshily along the distal three-quarters of the ventral tibiale, independent of the tibialis posterior.
occurrences.note: Moved here from the forelimb record of the same name, where it had been filed for want of a pes counterpart.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed, as in the hand. The one contrahens the human foot retains is the adductor hallucis, scored on [[contrahentes-digitorum-pes]]; the long head of the contrahens layer is gone from both limbs.

homology.notes: Separated from the forelimb record of the same name because Blotto et al. (2020) and Walthall & Ashley-Ross (2006) both describe hand and foot muscles under this one name.

muscles.name: Flexor accessorius lateralis (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Dorsal side of the plantar fascia.
consensus.action: Pronates the foot.

occurrences.name: Flexor accessorius lateralis
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fibres run diagonally toward the anterior side of the foot. The forelimb counterpart takes the distal ulna as well as the carpals; this one is confined to the tarsus.

occurrences.name: Quadratus plantae
occurrences.action: Redirects the pull of the long digital flexor along the axis of the foot.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Anterior calcaneus and the long plantar ligament, inserting not on bone but on the flexor digitorum longus tendons. **The hand lost this muscle and the foot kept it**, which is the opposite of the digital-extensor case and the reverse of what a strict serial reading of the two limbs would predict. Its job is purely mechanical: the long flexor enters the sole obliquely from the medial side, and this muscle pulls its tendons straight before they reach the toes.

muscles.name: Flexor accessorius medialis (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.origin: Distal fibula, the fibulare and the intermedium.
consensus.insertion: Plantar fascia.
consensus.action: Pronates the foot.

occurrences.name: Flexor accessorius medialis
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Parallel to the lateral accessory and sharing its insertion, differing only in taking a more proximal origin that reaches the fibula.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed. Only the lateral member of the pair survives in a human foot, as the quadratus plantae; see [[flexor-accessorius-lateralis-pes]].

muscles.name: Intermetatarsales
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Metatarsal of the adjacent digit.
consensus.action: Adducts the metatarsals and the digits attached to them.

occurrences.name: Intermetatarsales
occurrences.note: These muscles form the web-like structures between the digits. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Extend further distally on the fibular side of each metatarsal — an asymmetry the intermetacarpales of the hand do not show.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). As in the hand, the human interossei of the foot are scored once — on [[flexores-breves-profundi-pes]] — and the claim this record has on them is recorded rather than acted on. Howell (1936) found the relationship between Interossei, Intermetacarpales, Dorsometacarpales and Contrahentes digitorum unclear across tetrapods, and nothing in a human table resolves it.

muscles.name: Extensores digitorum breves (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.origin: Distal tarsals at the base of each digit.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal surface of the proximal end of the terminal phalanx, by long tendons.
consensus.action: Extends the digits.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.note: Five slips, one per digit. The muscular part reaches only about two-thirds along the metatarsal; the tendon continues to the terminal phalanx. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Five slips against three in the manus, which serves digits II-IV only. The difference is the salamander hand's missing digit V, not a difference in the muscle layer.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: Extensor digitorum brevis superficialis arises from the astragalar hollow and lateral calcaneum; the deep layer arises from the proximodorsal metatarsals, whose fine striations run parallel to the metatarsal long axis.
occurrences.note: Moved here from the forelimb record of the same name, where it had been filed for want of a pes counterpart.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.origin: Two proximal heads from the dorsal depression on the astragalus; the hallucal slip from the dorsal aspect of metatarsal I; the digit II, III and IV slips from the dorsal or dorsolateral aspects of metatarsals II, III and the astragalocalcaneum lip respectively.
occurrences.insertion: Proximodorsal lip of each phalanx of digits III and IV from the tarsal heads; the proximodorsal lips of phalanges I-1 and I-2 from the hallucal slip; the proximodorsal lips of the phalanges of digits II and III from their own slips; the ungual of digit IV with accessory insertions on IV-2 to IV-4.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana. Hattori & Tsuihiji's separation of the interossei dorsales out of this complex is what makes the remainder countable; the slips left here are the ones arising from the tarsus or from the digit's OWN metatarsal, and those arising from the metatarsal medial to the digit are on `interossei-dorsales-pes`.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.origin: Dorsal depression on the astragalus, with two additional slips beyond the Iguana condition; the digit II and III slips from the dorsal and dorsolateral aspects of metatarsals II and III.
occurrences.insertion: Proximodorsal lips of the phalanges of digits III and IV, and — unlike Iguana — of digits I and II as well; in Varanus an additional tendinous insertion on the medial margin of the distal metatarsal III.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus indicus. **Two more slips than the iguana**, serving digits I and II, which is the second scored difference between Hattori & Tsuihiji's two squamates.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum brevis + abductor hallucis
occurrences.origin: Depression on the dorsal aspect of distal tarsal IV; the hallucal member (m. abductor hallucis) from the dorsal aspect of metatarsal I with an additional origin on phalanx I-1.
occurrences.insertion: Merging distally with the interossei dorsales and inserting with them on the proximodorsal lips of the distal phalanges of digits III and IV; the hallucal member on the proximodorsal lips of I-1 and I-2.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Chelydra serpentina. The tarsal origin is on distal tarsal IV rather than on the astragalus as in squamates and crocodilians — the one place Hattori & Tsuihiji concede the turtle origin is 'slightly different', while still following Gadow (1882) in calling it homologous. Trachemys adds an origin from DT III and an insertion on digit II (Walker 1973). The additional hallucal origin on I-1 is this animal's; Trachemys has it on DT I instead.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum I, II et III
occurrences.origin: Depression on the dorsal aspect of the astragalus; the hallucal slip from the dorsal aspect of metatarsal I; the digit II, III and IV slips from the dorsal surfaces of metatarsals II, III and IV.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsally on digits I-III through the dorsal aponeurosis; the hallucal slip on the proximodorsal lips of I-1 and I-2; each digital slip on the proximodorsal lip of every phalanx of its digit.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Paleosuchus palpebrosus. Suzuki et al. (2011) kept this muscle separate in crocodilians as m. extensor digitorum I, II et III; Hattori & Tsuihiji propose extensor digitorum brevis as the standard name for it and its homologues, because the digit I-II bellies are sometimes missing in lepidosaurs and the digit IV belly in crocodilians, so a name fixed to a digit list does not travel. In Caiman the origin is not on the astragalus but on soft tissue between it and the calcaneum.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum I, II et III
occurrences.origin: Depression on the dorsal aspect of the astragalus, plus the dorsal surfaces of metatarsals I-IV for the digital slips.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsally on digits I-III by the dorsal aponeurosis, and on the proximodorsal lips of the phalanges of each digit served.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Extensores breves digitorum III et IV
occurrences.origin: Dorsal aspect of the distal half of the tarsometatarsus, the digit III origin marked by a slightly depressed rugose surface and the digit IV origin by a sulcus lateral to it.
occurrences.insertion: Proximodorsal lip of phalanx III-1, and the medial aspect of IV-1 — the latter tendon running through the canalis interosseus distalis and its insertion marked by a tuber.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus gallus. **Two members left of five.** The extensor digitorum brevis and the extensor hallucis brevis are both absent in birds, and only the digit III and IV slips survive, both now arising from the tarsometatarsus. Hattori & Tsuihiji use the digit III member as a test case for their metatarsal-identity reasoning: its origin on the middle of the distal half of the tarsometatarsus corresponds to metatarsal III, not to metatarsal II, which is why they refuse it as the homologue of the non-avian interosseous dorsalis digiti III.

occurrences.name: Extensores breves digitorum III et IV
occurrences.origin: Dorsal aspect of the distal half of the tarsometatarsus.
occurrences.insertion: Proximodorsal lip of III-1 and the medial aspect of IV-1.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Grus japonensis. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis
occurrences.action: Extend the metatarsophalangeal joints of digits 1-4.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Both from the superolateral surface of the calcaneus; brevis to the extensor expansions of toes 1-4, hallucis brevis to the dorsum of the proximal phalanx of the hallux. **The hand lost this layer and the foot kept it** — see the `extensores-digitorum-breves` row, scored absent for the human hand. Both limbs of one animal, one retaining the ancestral short extensor sheet and the other not, which is a caution against reading the two limbs as versions of each other.

muscles.name: Abductor et extensor digiti I (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal intrinsic layer of the pes, preaxial margin.

consensus.origin: Proximal tarsals of the preaxial ankle.
consensus.insertion: Lateral face of the first metatarsal and its phalanx.
consensus.action: Abducts and extends the first metatarsal and its digit.

occurrences.name: Abductor et extensor digiti I
occurrences.note: The paper's text calls these 'bones of the wrist' in the hindlimb section, evidently a slip for the ankle; the muscle is figured in the pes. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The preaxial counterpart of the abductor digiti minimi at the other margin of the foot. Its forelimb equivalent takes the radiale and intermedium.

occurrences.name: Adductor et extensor hallucis et indicus
occurrences.origin: A broad, flat or slightly depressed surface on the dorsolateral aspect of the distal fibula, and the medial half of a slight convex lip at the proximolateral margin of the tarsal facet of the astragalocalcaneum.
occurrences.insertion: Medial margin and laterodistal shaft of metatarsal I, and metatarsal II.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana. The record's name comes from Russell & Bauer's for this muscle, so this is the animal it was named from.

occurrences.name: Adductor et extensor hallucis et indicus
occurrences.origin: Dorsolateral aspect of the distal fibula and the proximolateral margin of the tarsal facet of the astragalocalcaneum.
occurrences.insertion: Metatarsal I only, the insertion marked by rugosity on the bone.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus indicus. **The insertion is narrower than the iguana's** — MT I alone, where Iguana takes MT I and MT II, and Chamaeleo takes only MT II (Russell & Bauer 2008). Three squamates, three different digits for one muscle, which is the position-versus-identity question asked inside a clade.

occurrences.name: Extensor hallucis proprius
occurrences.origin: Distal end of the fibula, the origin marked as a clear depression on the distodorsal margin of the bone, and the dorsal aspect of the astragalocalcaneum.
occurrences.insertion: Lateral sides of the distal third of metatarsal I and the proximal half of phalanx I-1, and the medial side of the mid-shaft of I-1.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Chelydra serpentina. The tarsal origin is absent in Trachemys (Walker 1973), so it varies within turtles.

occurrences.name: Adductor hallucis dorsalis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal aspect of the distal fibula.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal aspect of the proximal third of the shaft of metatarsal I, just proximal to the tibialis anterior insertion; the distal border of the insertion is marked by a transverse ridge on metatarsal I.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Paleosuchus palpebrosus. No tarsal origin here, unlike the squamates and the turtle.

occurrences.name: Adductor hallucis dorsalis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal aspect of the distal fibula.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal aspect of the proximal third of metatarsal I, bounded distally by a transverse ridge.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Suzuki et al. (2011) described the insertion as divided into two sites in this species; Hattori & Tsuihiji dissected the same species and did not find the division, and read the disagreement as intraspecific variation rather than error.

occurrences.name: Adductor hallucis dorsalis
occurrences.note: Gallus gallus. Absent. Hutchinson (2002) treated this muscle as the homologue of the avian m. extensor hallucis longus; Hattori & Tsuihiji reject that and place the avian muscle with the extensor hallucis brevis instead, on `extensores-digitorum-breves-pes`. So the absence here is a positive claim about where the avian muscle went, not silence.

occurrences.name: Adductor hallucis dorsalis
occurrences.note: Grus japonensis. Absent, as in Gallus.

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.action: Abducts and flexes the great toe.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Medial side of the calcaneal tuberosity to the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the hallux — the preaxial marginal muscle of the sole, in the position its forelimb counterpart the abductor pollicis brevis occupies in the palm.

muscles.name: Abductor digiti minimi (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; intrinsic layer of the pes, postaxial margin.

consensus.insertion: Fibulare, the postaxial distal tarsal, and the base of the fifth metatarsal.
consensus.action: Abducts the fifth metatarsal and its digit.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti V
occurrences.note: Basale V is scored as a distal tarsal; the paper's more specific term is kept here rather than given its own element. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: An extensive fleshy insertion across three skeletal elements. The manus counterpart serves digit IV, because the salamander hand has lost digit V — the same muscle at the same margin, on a differently numbered digit.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti minimi
occurrences.attachmentNote: A large muscle with fleshy origin over almost the whole dorsolateral fibulare, inserting by short tendon on the dorsal and proximal metatarsal V.
occurrences.note: Moved here from the forelimb record of the same name, where it had been filed for want of a pes counterpart.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti minimi
occurrences.action: Abducts the fifth digit.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Medial and lateral sides of the calcaneal tuberosity to the lateral base of the proximal phalanx of digit V — the postaxial marginal muscle, the mirror of the abductor hallucis across the sole. In the hand the equivalent muscle arises from the pisiform, a sesamoid the foot has no counterpart for, so the two limbs reach the same arrangement from different bones.

homology.teaching: Postaxial position and digit number disagree between hand and foot in salamanders. Matching by number would pair this muscle with nothing; matching by position pairs it with the manual extensor lateralis digiti IV.

muscles.name: Interossei dorsales (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep dorsal mass of the pes.
synonyms: mm. interossei dorsales digiti II-IV (Hattori & Tsuihiji 2021)
part of mm. extensores breves (Russell & Bauer 2008, for lepidosaurs)
part of mm. interossei dorsales (Walker 1973, for turtles)
m. abductor digiti II (Aves; Vanden Berge & Zweers 1993)

consensus.origin: Dorsal or lateroplantar aspect of the metatarsal one position medial to the digit of insertion.
consensus.insertion: Proximodorsal lip of the phalanges of that digit, largely through the dorsal aponeurosis.
consensus.action: Abducts digits II and III and adducts digit IV, if the slips act independently of the short extensors they fuse with distally.
consensus.innervation: Deep fibular nerve; superficial in some crocodilian accounts.

occurrences.name: Interossei dorsales digiti II-IV (as slips of mm. extensores digitores breves)
occurrences.origin: Ridge-like longitudinal rugose areas: the digit II slip from metatarsal I, the digit III slip tendinously from the lateral margin of the proximal half of metatarsal II, the digit IV slip from the lateral margin of the proximal half of metatarsal III.
occurrences.insertion: Each forms the medial portion of the dorsal aponeurosis of its digit and inserts on the proximodorsal lip of each phalanx; the digit IV slip inserts medially on the proximal margin of each phalanx.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana. Russell & Bauer (2008) read these as portions of mm. extensores breves; Hattori & Tsuihiji separate them on the rugose longitudinal ridges each arises from, which are visible on the bone and are the correlate for the whole series.

occurrences.name: Interossei dorsales digiti II-III
occurrences.origin: Ridge-like longitudinal rugose areas on metatarsals I and II.
occurrences.insertion: The medial portion of the dorsal aponeurosis of digits II and III, on the proximodorsal lip of each phalanx; in Varanus an additional tendinous insertion on the medial margin of distal metatarsal III.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus indicus. The digit IV member was found in Iguana and not here. Russell & Bauer described the digit III belly as arising from the lateral aspect of the DISTAL portion of metatarsal II; Hattori & Tsuihiji find it proximal and treat the difference as intraspecific variation.

occurrences.name: Interossei dorsales digiti II-IV
occurrences.origin: Rugosities on the proximomedial margin of the dorsal aspect of metatarsals I, II and III, the digit II member also from the astragalocalcaneum, distal tarsal I and phalanx II-1, and the digit IV member also from distal tarsal IV and phalanx IV-1.
occurrences.insertion: The distal phalanges of digits II, III and IV by a dorsal aponeurosis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Chelydra serpentina. Walker (1973) already used the name mm. interossei dorsales for the turtle series but did not distinguish it from the short extensors it merges with; the accessory origins on the first phalanges are this animal's, and Trachemys lacks several of them.

occurrences.name: Interossei dorsales digiti II-IV
occurrences.origin: Digit II member from the depression on the lateroplantar aspect of metatarsal I with a stout tendinous structure; digit III member from the rugose surface on the dorsal and lateral aspects of the lateral margin of proximal metatarsal II; digit IV member from the depression on the lateroplantar aspect of the proximal-most shaft of metatarsal III.
occurrences.insertion: Each joins the dorsal aponeurosis of its digit, but most fibres end on the proximodorsal lip of the first phalanx.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Paleosuchus palpebrosus. The crocodilian members are the clearest of the series: named separately by Suzuki et al. (2011), carrying their own tendons, and — for the digit III member — innervated differently from the short extensors it lies beside. Hattori & Tsuihiji note the digit IV member is absent from Cong et al.'s (1998) account and so is possibly absent in Alligator sinensis.

occurrences.name: Interossei dorsales digiti II-IV
occurrences.origin: Depressions and rugosities on the lateral aspects of metatarsals I, II and III.
occurrences.insertion: The dorsal aponeurosis of digits II, III and IV, most fibres ending on the proximodorsal lip of the first phalanx of each.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti II
occurrences.origin: Lateral aspect of metatarsal I and the dorsomedial aspect of the tarsometatarsus, the tarsometatarsal origin marked by an oblique groove on the medial aspect of the shaft and by the fossa metatarsi I.
occurrences.insertion: Medioplantar tubercle at the proximal end of phalanx II-1.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus gallus. **One of three members survives in birds, and it closes an orphan correlate.** The digit II member persists as m. abductor digiti II, keeping the metatarsal I origin, the digit II insertion and the deep fibular nerve that identify the series; the digit III and IV members are absent, and Hattori & Tsuihiji explicitly refuse the avian extensores breves digiti III and IV as their homologues because those arise from the wrong metatarsal and extend rather than adduct. The fossa metatarsi I is one of the fifteen osteological correlates GAPS §3 listed as carrying no muscle.

parts.name: Interosseous dorsalis digiti II (m. abductor digiti II)
Interosseous dorsalis digiti III
parts.note: Absent in birds on Hattori & Tsuihiji's reading; the avian m. extensor brevis digiti III is not accepted as its homologue.

parts.name: Interosseous dorsalis digiti IV
parts.note: Absent in birds; the avian m. extensor brevis digiti IV is scored on extensores-digitorum-breves-pes.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti II
occurrences.origin: Lateral aspect of metatarsal I and the dorsomedial aspect of the tarsometatarsus at the fossa metatarsi I.
occurrences.insertion: Medioplantar tubercle at the proximal end of phalanx II-1.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Grus japonensis. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). The human dorsal interossei of the foot are scored once, on [[flexores-breves-profundi-pes]], whose mammalian synonymy names them. This record exists because Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) separate a dorsal interosseous series from the short digital extensors in sauropsids — a distinction drawn on archosaur and lepidosaur material, not on mammals — so whether the human muscles belong here as well is not something Gest's table can settle. Uncertain rather than a second copy of the same observation.

homology.notes:
**A series separated from the short digital extensors by Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021), not a renaming of them.** In lepidosaurs and turtles these slips had been described as portions of mm. extensores breves (Russell & Bauer 2008) or of mm. interossei dorsales without being distinguished from them (Walker 1973). Their case for a distinct series is that each slip arises from the proximolateral aspect of the metatarsal MEDIALLY ADJACENT to the digit it serves, carries a stout tendon of its own, and forms the medial portion of that digit's extensor — so most fibres end on the proximomedial margins of the phalanges and the slips would act as abductors of digits II-III and an adductor of digit IV. They fuse distally with the short extensors, which is why they were missed. The distinction was previously unknown in non-archosaurian sauropsids and is what lets the avian short extensors be compared with the non-avian ones at all.

Kept separate from `intermetatarsales`, which runs metatarsal to metatarsal, forms the interdigital webs and takes the lateral plantar nerve — a different muscle by attachment and by innervation, not a different name for this one.

**Scored so far only from Hattori & Tsuihiji's seven sauropsids**, so absence elsewhere in this dataset is unsampled rather than observed.
homology.openQuestion: Only the digit II member survives in birds, as m. abductor digiti II. Hattori & Tsuihiji reject the avian mm. extensores breves digiti III and IV as homologues of the digit III and IV members on the grounds that their tarsometatarsal origins correspond to the wrong metatarsal and that they extend rather than adduct. Is that a loss of two muscles, or a fusion into the avian short extensors?
